support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex: The expression $x\in A$ is a primitive membership assertion.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Set theory begins with objects called sets and a primitive relation expressing
membership of one object in another.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Primitive means that set and membership are not defined in terms of simpler
concepts. Their meaning is fixed implicitly by stating the axioms they must
obey. This is the standard approach in formal mathematics: rules of behavior replace
informal definitions.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
All subsequent notions---subsets, ordered pairs, relations, functions,
number systems---are \emph{definitions} introduced within this axiomatic
framework. Every proved result is a \emph{theorem} derived logically from the
axioms via the rules of inference.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The axioms are not statements to be proved, but rules specifying how $\in$
behaves and which sets are permitted to exist. From this point onward, set
theory functions as the underlying language of mathematics: all reasoning
about mathematical objects is ultimately grounded in these axioms, even when
they are not cited explicitly.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Separation is a schema: one axiom instance per definable property $\varphi$.
It carves out subsets of an already-existing set. Replacement is strictly
stronger: it can produce sets whose elements are not already contained in any
pre-existing set, allowing the construction of large stages of the cumulative
hierarchy.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The Axiom of Choice is equivalent to many statements used later in analysis,
including Zorn's Lemma, the well-ordering theorem, and the statement that every
surjective function has a right inverse. It is independent of the other ZFC
axioms.

Two sets $A$ and $B$ are \emph{equal}, written $A = B$, if they have the same
elements:
\[
A = B \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \forall x \, (x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B).
\]
Equivalently, $A = B \iff (A \subseteq B \land B \subseteq A)$.

complement operation over a universal set of all sets.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Equivalent representatives of a complex class have the same real and imaginary coordinates.


The construction of \(\mathbb{C}\) completes the standard ladder of number
systems in this volume:
\[
\mathbb{N}\subseteq\mathbb{W}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}\subseteq
\mathbb{Q}\subseteq\mathbb{R}\subseteq\mathbb{C}.
\]
The final step sacrifices order compatibility in exchange for algebraic power:
\(-1\) now has a square root.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The complex field cannot be equipped with an ordered-field order compatible

\(i^2=-1\), and \(-1<0\) in the real subfield.

complex classes agree. Thus addition descends to a binary operation on
$\mathbb{C}$.

nodes.name: Compatibility of the Embedding Chain
nodes.statement_display: Let $\iota_{1}:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{W}$, $\iota_{2}:\mathbb{W}\to\mathbb{Z}$, $\iota_{3}:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Q}$, and $\iota_{4}:\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{R}$ be the canonical embeddings. For every $n\in\mathbb{N}$ the composite $(\iota_{4}\circ\iota_{3}\circ\iota_{2}\circ\iota_{1})(n)$ is the real number identified with $n$, and the composite preserves the arithmetic and order carried by the source system. Hence arithmetic computed in any system agrees with arithmetic on its image in $\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Structure-Preserving Map
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A$ and $B$ be ordered arithmetic systems with a specified common source
structure: selected constants, selected operations, and a strict order. A map
$\varphi:A\to B$ is \emph{structure-preserving} exactly when it preserves each
selected constant and, for every selected binary operation $\star$ and all
$a,a'\in A$,
\[
\varphi(a\star_A a')=\varphi(a)\star_B\varphi(a'),
\]
and $a<_A a' \Longrightarrow \varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a')$.

\Bigl(\text{every selected constant is preserved}\\
&\qquad\land\ \text{every selected operation is preserved}\\
&\qquad\land \forall a,a'\in A\;(a<_A a' \Rightarrow \varphi(a)<_B\varphi(a'))\Bigr).

\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A structure-preserving map carries the chosen arithmetic and order from $A$
into $B$ without distortion. The choice of structure matters: the positive
part of $\mathbb{W}$ carries the Peano successor from $\mathbb{N}$, while
the later ring and field embeddings focus on $0$, $1$, addition,
multiplication, and order. A structure-preserving map need not be injective;
collapsing distinct elements is still allowed at this stage. Injectivity is
added separately to obtain an embedding.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.] An embedding can fail by losing distinctness, by failing to preserve selected algebraic structure, or by failing to preserve and reflect order.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
An embedding is the precise meaning of ``$A$ sits inside $B$.'' It is injective, so distinct elements stay distinct; it preserves the arithmetic and reflects the order, so the copy of $A$ inside $B$ behaves exactly as $A$ did. This is what licenses treating $2\in\mathbb{N}$ and $2\in\mathbb{R}$ as ``the same number.''


Most embeddings after $\mathbb{W}$ transport the \emph{ordered ring/field}
structure: constants, the two operations, and order. The first bridge
$\mathbb{N}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{W}$ is slightly different because
$\mathbb{N}$ is one-based and carries Peano successor. That local theorem is
proved in the whole-number chapter. In every case, induction is not transported
to the larger target: the phrase ``the naturals sit inside the integers'' must
not be read as carrying induction across all of $\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: Embeddings Identify a System with Its Image
nodes.statement_display:
Let $\varphi:A\to B$ be an embedding of ordered arithmetic systems relative to
a selected source structure. Then the corestriction $\varphi:A\to\varphi(A)$
is an isomorphism onto its image: it is a bijection that preserves and reflects
the selected constants, operations, and order. Consequently $A$ may be
identified with the corresponding substructure $\varphi(A)\subseteq B$.

nodes.name: Extended Real Addition
nodes.statement_display:

real addition when $x,y\in\mathbb{R}$, and satisfies
\[
x+(+\infty)=+\infty,\qquad x+(-\infty)=-\infty
\]
whenever these expressions are defined.

defined by
\[
-(+\infty)=-\infty,\qquad -(-\infty)=+\infty.
\]
Subtraction is defined by
\[
x-y=x+(-y)
\]
whenever the right-hand side is defined.

nodes.name: Extended Real Multiplication
nodes.statement_display:
Extended multiplication agrees with ordinary real multiplication on finite
inputs. If $x\in\mathbb{R}$ is positive, then
\[
x(+\infty)=+\infty,\qquad x(-\infty)=-\infty,
\]
and if $x\in\mathbb{R}$ is negative, then
\[
x(+\infty)=-\infty,\qquad x(-\infty)=+\infty.
\]
Products of two infinite endpoints follow the corresponding sign rule.

nodes.name: Extended Real Interval
nodes.statement_display:
A set $I\subseteq\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is an \emph{extended real interval} if
whenever $x,z\in I$ and $x\le y\le z$ in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, then
$y\in I$.

nodes.name: Order on the Extended Reals
nodes.statement_display:
The order on $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ extends the order on $\mathbb{R}$ by
requiring
\[
-\infty\le x\le +\infty
\]
for every $x\in\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, and by preserving the usual order
between finite elements.

nodes.name: Classification of Intervals in $\mathbb{R}$
nodes.statement_display:
Every interval in $\mathbb{R}$ is one of the standard interval types:
\[
(a,b),\ [a,b],\ (a,b],\ [a,b),\ (a,\infty),\ [a,\infty),
\]
\[
(-\infty,b),\ (-\infty,b],\ \mathbb{R},\ \varnothing,
\]
including degenerate one-point intervals.

nodes.name: Positive cone
nodes.statement_display:
Let $K$ be an arithmetic system with addition, multiplication, and zero. A
subset $P\subset K$ is called a \emph{positive cone} if it satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item if $a,b\in P$, then $a+b\in P$;
  \item if $a,b\in P$, then $ab\in P$;
  \item for every $a\in K$, exactly one of the following holds:
  \[
  a\in P,
  \qquad
  a=0,
  \qquad
  -a\in P.
  \]
\end{enumerate}
The strict order associated to $P$ is
\[
a<b \iff b-a\in P.
\]

Z=\{0\}\sqcup P\sqcup N,
\]
where \(P\) is generated from a first positive element by repeated successor
and \(N\) is generated from a first negative element by repeated predecessor.

nodes.name: Two-sided induction and recursion
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(A\) be a predicate on \(Z\). If \(A(0)\), \(A(x)\Rightarrow
A(\mathsf{succ}(x))\), and \(A(x)\Rightarrow A(\mathsf{pred}(x))\)
for every \(x\in Z\), then \(A(x)\) holds for every \(x\in Z\).
Moreover, any value at zero and mutually inverse successor and predecessor
steps determine a unique recursive function out of \(Z\).

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
A property holds everywhere on \(Z\) once it holds at zero and propagates both
forward and backward; a recursive definition on \(Z\) is determined by its
zero value and compatible forward and backward steps.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This is why the ray decomposition matters. To prove something for every
integer, prove it at zero, along the positive ray, and along the negative ray.
To define an operation recursively, the forward and backward clauses must
agree at the places where the rays meet zero.

support_blocks.body_tex:
There is a structure-preserving bijection between the two-sided construction
and the canonical integer system.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This is the comparison theorem that prevents the construction from becoming a
new arithmetic universe. It is a different presentation of the same integers.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Lean verification record. Source: Iwanu{\'s}; Wybraniec. Formalizes
\hyperref[thm:two-sided-integers-isomorphic-to-z]{the comparison theorem}.
Lean modules: \texttt{LRA.VolumeII.Integers.Polish.LandauWorkup} and
\texttt{LRA.VolumeII.Integers.Polish.DiscreteIntegerStructure}. Declarations:
\texttt{Z\_iso\_Int}, \texttt{categoricity}. Status: checked against
\texttt{lra-lean}.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
The formal-difference construction begins with pairs and an equivalence
relation. Tao emphasizes expressions \(a{--}b\); Mendelson emphasizes
equivalence classes of pairs and develops more abstract algebra around them.
The two-sided construction begins instead with the geometry of the integer
line. It avoids quotient well-definedness, but it requires explicit recursive
definitions and many transport lemmas for successor and predecessor.

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
This section is therefore not a replacement for the standard construction. It
is a worked example of construction verification: choose a target, propose
data, state the axioms, build operations, prove the laws, and finally compare
the result with the already accepted system.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x=y&\Longrightarrow f(x)=f(y),\\
x=y&\Longrightarrow \bigl(P(x)\Longleftrightarrow P(y)\bigr),\\
x=x'\land y=y'
&\Longrightarrow \bigl(R(x,y)\Longleftrightarrow R(x',y')\bigr),\\
x=x'\land y=y'
&\Longrightarrow x\mathbin{O}y=x'\mathbin{O}y'.
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Respecting equality is automatic. Respecting a nontrivial equivalence relation
is not automatic; that is why quotient constructions must prove separate
respect lemmas before operations, predicates, or relations descend to classes.

nodes.name: Mendelson 4.3 --- Positivity set construction
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(R\) be an integral domain with \(0\neq 1\). If
\(\mathcal{P}\subseteq R\) excludes \(0\), trichotomizes each element by
membership in \(\mathcal{P}\), equality to \(0\), or membership of its
negative, and is closed under addition and multiplication, then
\[
  x<y \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y-x\in\mathcal{P}
\]
defines an ordered integral domain whose positive set is \(\mathcal{P}\).

nodes.name: Mendelson 5.3 --- GCD and Bezout form
nodes.statement_display:
For integers \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\), not both zero, a greatest common divisor
exists. Moreover, the greatest common divisor may be written in Bezout form
\[
  d = x\alpha+y\beta
\]
for some integers \(x,y\).

nodes.name: Mendelson 5.4 --- Relative primeness criterion
nodes.statement_display:
Two integers are relatively prime if and only if their greatest common divisor
is a unit, equivalently if and only if \(1\) is an integer linear combination
of the two integers up to sign.

nodes.name: Mendelson 5.6 --- Euclid's lemma

\[

  \quad\text{or}\quad
  \rho\mid\beta.
\]

nodes.name: Mendelson 5.7--5.9 --- Unique prime factorization
nodes.statement_display:
Every nonzero nonunit integer factors into primes, and this factorization is
unique up to reordering and multiplication of factors by units.

positive elements contains a least element.

nodes.name: Mendelson 9.8 --- Uniqueness of \(\mathbb{Z}\)
nodes.statement_display:
Any two well-ordered integral domains are isomorphic. In particular,
\(\mathbb{Z}\) is unique up to isomorphism as a well-ordered integral domain.

nodes.name: Tao integer expression
nodes.statement_display:
An integer expression in Tao's construction is a placeholder \(a {-\!\!-} b\)
with \(a,b\in\mathbb{N}\). Two placeholders are equal when
\[
  a {-\!\!-} b = c {-\!\!-} d
  \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
  a+d=c+b.
\]
The collection of equivalence classes is denoted \(\mathbb{Z}\).

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The definition replaces the circular phrase \(a-b\) with a formal pair and an
equality criterion that only uses arithmetic already available in
\(\mathbb{N}\). The construction pays the equivalence-relation cost once and
then supports uniform definitions of operations on classes.

support_blocks.title: Notation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The symbol \(--\) is scaffolding notation. After subtraction is defined on
\(\mathbb{Z}\), the expression \(a {-\!\!-} b\) agrees with the genuine
difference \(a-b\).

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
This presentation contrasts with the signed-natural description of integers.
The signed-natural picture is intuitive, but it forces repeated case splits
for addition, multiplication, and order. The quotient construction centralizes
those checks in the equivalence relation and well-definedness lemmas.

nodes.name: Tao 4.1.3 --- Addition and multiplication are well-defined
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(a,b,a',b',c,d\in\mathbb{N}\). If
\((a {-\!\!-} b)=(a' {-\!\!-} b')\), then
\begin{align*}
  (a {-\!\!-} b) + (c {-\!\!-} d)
    &= (a' {-\!\!-} b') + (c {-\!\!-} d), \\
  (a {-\!\!-} b)(c {-\!\!-} d)
    &= (a' {-\!\!-} b')(c {-\!\!-} d),
\end{align*}
and similarly when the second representative is replaced by an equal one.

nodes.name: Tao 4.1.5 --- Trichotomy of integers
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(x\in\mathbb{Z}\). Exactly one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(x=0\).
  \item \(x=n\) for some positive natural number \(n\).
  \item \(x=-n\) for some positive natural number \(n\).
\end{enumerate}
In the second case \(x\) is positive, and in the third case \(x\) is negative.

nodes.name: Tao 4.1.11 --- Properties of order on \(\mathbb{Z}\)
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}\). Then:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(a>b\) if and only if \(a-b\) is a positive natural number.
  \item If \(a>b\), then \(a+c>b+c\).
  \item If \(a>b\) and \(c\) is a positive integer, then \(ac>bc\).
  \item If \(a>b\), then \(-a<-b\).
  \item If \(a>b\) and \(b>c\), then \(a>c\).
  \item Exactly one of \(a>b\), \(a<b\), and \(a=b\) holds.
\end{enumerate}

using the algebraic laws already established for \(\mathbb{Z}\).

nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For each $m \in P$, define the function
\[
f_m : P \to P
\]
to be the unique function satisfying
\[
f_m(1)=S(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(f_m(S(n))=S(f_m(n))).
\]
For $m,n \in P$, define
\[
m+n \coloneqq f_m(n).
\]

right-input map. The value $m+1$ is set to be the successor of $m$, and each

nodes.name: Addition Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
f_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
f_m(1)=S(m)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(f_m(S(n))=S(f_m(n))).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m+n \coloneqq f_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The theorem shows that the recursive clauses for addition determine exactly one
right-input map for each fixed left input. The addition operation is therefore
not assumed; it is constructed from the successor map by recursion.


This is the house-style well-definedness form of addition obtained by applying
the Peano recursion theorem in the manner of Feferman's construction of
arithmetic operations \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Because every element of $P$ is at least one successor step, the sum $m+n$
lies strictly beyond $n$. The theorem rules out additive cycles and is a
standard tool for order arguments on the natural numbers.


This is the house-style form of the additive non-return theorem in
\citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{N}$ Is Closed, Associative, and Commutative Under Addition
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $+$ on $P$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b \in P$.
  \item \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
  $(a+b)+c = a+(b+c)$.
  \item \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a+b = b+a$.
  \item \textbf{Left cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $a+b = a+c$ then $b=c$.
  \item \textbf{Right cancellation.} For all $a,b,c \in P$, if $b+a = c+a$ then $b=c$.
\end{enumerate}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This theorem is a packaging result. It names the algebraic structure that
has been proved piece by piece: the three individual theorems on associativity,
commutativity, and cancellation together certify that $(P,+)$ is a cancellative
commutative semigroup. There is no additive identity in $P$ because $P$ has
no element $0$ with $0+n=n$ for all $n$; the smallest element under addition
is $1$, not an identity.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{N}$ Is a Commutative Monoid Under Multiplication
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. The binary operation $\cdot$ on $P$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Closure.} For all $a,b \in P$, $a \cdot b \in P$.
  \item \textbf{Associativity.} For all $a,b,c \in P$,
  $(a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)$.
  \item \textbf{Commutativity.} For all $a,b \in P$,
  $a \cdot b = b \cdot a$.
  \item \textbf{Identity.} For all $a \in P$,
  $1 \cdot a = a = a \cdot 1$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently $(P, \cdot, 1)$ is a commutative monoid.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{N}$ Is a Semiring
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. Then $(P,+,\cdot)$ satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item $(P,+)$ is a commutative semigroup.
  \item $(P,\cdot,1)$ is a commutative monoid.
  \item Multiplication distributes over addition: for all $a,b,c \in P$,
  \[
  a \cdot (b+c) = (a \cdot b) + (a \cdot c).
  \]
\end{enumerate}

support_blocks.body_tex:
A semiring packages the interaction of two operations without requiring
additive inverses. The natural numbers are the canonical example of a semiring
that is not a ring: they satisfy every ring axiom except the existence of
additive inverses, which fails because there is no element $-1$ in $P$.
The integers are the smallest ring extending $P$ that repairs this failure.

\[
g_m : P \to P
\]
to be the unique function satisfying
\[
g_m(1)=m
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(g_m(S(n))=g_m(n)+m).
\]
For $m,n \in P$, define
\[
m \cdot n \coloneqq g_m(n).
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  The definition fails only when a proposed value for $m \cdot n$ does not
  agree with the recursively generated function attached to the fixed left
  factor $m$. Once $g_m$ is determined, every incorrect candidate product is
  simply a value different from $g_m(n)$.

  \Longleftrightarrow

  \end{aligned}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Multiplication is introduced by fixing the left input and recursively
generating the right-input map. The value $m \cdot 1$ is initialized at $m$,
and each successor step in the right input adds one further copy of $m$.
Multiplication is therefore repeated addition.

nodes.name: Multiplication Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $m \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
g_m : P \to P
\]
such that
\[
g_m(1)=m
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(g_m(S(n))=g_m(n)+m).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(m,n) \longmapsto m \cdot n \coloneqq g_m(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{WellDefinedBinaryOperation}(\cdot_P,P).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The recursive clauses for multiplication determine exactly one right-input map
for each fixed left input. The multiplication operation is therefore
constructed from recursion and addition rather than assumed at the outset.


This is the house-style well-definedness form of multiplication obtained by
applying the Peano recursion theorem in the manner of Feferman's construction
of arithmetic operations \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

support_blocks.body_tex:

blocks of repeated addition. This is the bridge between the additive and
multiplicative structures.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The existing distributive law expands a sum in the right factor. This theorem
expands a sum in the left factor. It follows from right distributivity together
with commutativity of multiplication.


This is the house-style form of Feferman's left distributive law for
multiplication \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

nodes.name: Multiplication Distributes over Addition on Both Sides
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b,c \in P$,
\[
a\cdot(b+c)=(a\cdot b)+(a\cdot c)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad

\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]

  \item[Exposition.] The named branch below records the failed antisymmetry

Multiplication by a fixed natural number is an order embedding of the natural
numbers into themselves. It shifts strict inequalities forward without
collapsing distinct values.

to Feferman's order laws for products \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

other, or they coincide. Trichotomy is the theorem that upgrades the additive
comparison relation from a partial-order structure to a total order.

nodes.name: Natural-Number Order Is Total
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a,b \in P$,
\[
a \le b
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
b \le a.
\]
Consequently $\le$ is a total order on $P$.

nodes.name: Exponentiation on a Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For each $a \in P$, define the function
\[
h_a : P \to P
\]
to be the unique function satisfying
\[
h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).
\]
For $a,n \in P$, define
\[
a^n \coloneqq h_a(n).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Exponentiation is repeated multiplication in the same sense that multiplication
is repeated addition. The base $a$ is the fixed left factor; the exponent $n$
counts how many times $a$ is multiplied together. The recursive definition
propagates rightward: $a^1 = a$, $a^2 = a^1 \cdot a = a \cdot a$, and so on.

nodes.name: Exponentiation Is Well-Defined on a Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. For every $a \in P$, there exists a unique
function
\[
h_a:P\to P
\]
such that
\[
h_a(1)=a
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n \in P\;(h_a(S(n))=h_a(n)\cdot a).
\]
Consequently the rule
\[
(a,n)\longmapsto a^n\coloneqq h_a(n)
\]
defines a unique binary operation on $P$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The recursive clauses for exponentiation determine exactly one exponent map
for each fixed base. Exponentiation is therefore constructed from recursion
and multiplication rather than assumed as a primitive operation.


This is the house-style existence-and-uniqueness form of the recursive
definition of exponentiation in \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The base case $1 < 2 = 2^1$ holds by definition of $2$ and the strict order.
For the inductive step, assume $n < 2^n$. Then $2^{S(n)} = 2^n \cdot 2$.
Since $2^n > n \ge 1$, it follows that
$2^n \cdot 2 > n \cdot 2 = n + n > n + 1 = S(n)$,
where the last step uses $n \ge 1$ so $n + n > n + 1$. Hence $S(n) < 2^{S(n)}$.
The inequality $n < 2^n$ is the threshold that distinguishes the growth regimes
and reappears in every comparison between polynomial and exponential bounds.

modes.title: Exposition.
modes.body_tex:
The well-ordering principle would fail if some nonempty subset of $P$ had
  no least element. That means for every candidate minimum, a strictly smaller
  element of the subset exists, producing an infinite strictly descending
  chain in $P$. Induction rules this out.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The well-ordering principle is the order-theoretic complement to induction.
Induction says one can build up: start at $1$ and keep stepping forward.
Well-ordering says one can always descend to a minimum: any nonempty set has
a floor. Proof strategies that use well-ordering typically assume a property
fails somewhere, form the set of failures, extract its minimum by
well-ordering, and derive a contradiction from the minimality of that element.

nodes.name: Induction, Strong Induction, and Well-Ordering Are Equivalent
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system equipped with the order $\le$. The following
are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item The induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$, if
  $\varphi(1)$ holds and the successor step holds, then $\varphi(n)$ holds
  for all $n \in P$.
  \item The strong induction principle: for every predicate $\varphi$ on $P$,
  if $\varphi(k)$ holds for every $k<n$ implies $\varphi(n)$, then
  $\varphi(n)$ holds for every $n \in P$.
  \item The well-ordering principle: every nonempty subset of $P$ has a least
  element with respect to $\le$.
\end{enumerate}

Induction proves well-ordering by contrapositive: if a nonempty set $A$ had

least failure to derive a contradiction with the successor step.

nodes.name: Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
A \emph{Peano system} is a triple $(P,S,1)$ satisfying the following
conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item[\textbf{P1.}] $1 \in P$.
  \item[\textbf{P2.}] For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \in P$.
  \item[\textbf{P3.}] For every $n \in P$, $S(n) \neq 1$.
  \item[\textbf{P4.}] For all $m,n \in P$, if $S(m)=S(n)$ then $m=n$.
  \item[\textbf{P5.}] If $A \subseteq P$, $1 \in A$, and
  \[
    \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A),
  \]
  then $A=P$.
\end{enumerate}

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(P,S,1) \text{ is a Peano system}\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl(P \text{ is a set} \land 1 \in P
\land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \in P) \\
&\qquad \land \forall n \in P\;(S(n) \neq 1) \\
&\qquad \land \forall m,n \in P\;(S(m)=S(n) \Longrightarrow m=n) \\
&\qquad \land \forall A \subseteq P\;
\bigl((1 \in A \land
\forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A))
\Longrightarrow A=P\bigr)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  A triple $(P,S,1)$ fails to be a Peano system if the distinguished element
  does not lie in the underlying set, if the successor map leaves the set, if
  the successor hits $1$, if the successor identifies two distinct elements,
  or if there exists a proper subset of $P$ that contains $1$ and is closed
  under successor.
  \item[Axiom failure.]
  \[
  \neg\operatorname{PeanoSystem}(P,S,1).
  \]
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  \neg\,\text{$(P,S,1)$ is a Peano system}
  \Longrightarrow\;&
  1 \notin P \\
  &\lor \exists n \in P\;(S(n) \notin P) \\
  &\lor \exists n \in P\;(S(n)=1) \\
  &\lor \exists m,n \in P\;(m \neq n \land S(m)=S(n)) \\
  &\lor \exists A \subseteq P\;
  \bigl(1 \in A \land
  \forall n \in P\;(n \in A \Longrightarrow S(n) \in A)
  \land A \neq P\bigr).
  \end{aligned}
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A Peano system is the abstract data of counting: an underlying set, a
distinguished first element, and an injective successor operation whose image
omits the first element, together with an induction principle. The purpose of
the definition is to isolate the ambient object before the individual axioms
are recorded and used one by one.


The five displayed clauses are the house-style Peano-system presentation of
Peano's axiomatization of arithmetic \citep{PeanoArithmeticesPrincipia1889}.
They are stated here in structural form so that later definitions and proofs
can refer directly to the successor and induction clauses.

support_blocks.title: Source comparison
support_blocks.body_tex:
This definition corresponds closely to Definition 3.1 in
Feferman, where Peano systems are introduced as the abstract structural
framework underlying the positive integers. The present notes expand the
definition into explicit quantified, failure-mode, and decomposition forms in
order to support later logical analysis and dependency extraction.
\citet{FefermanNumberSystems1964}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The Peano axioms are not merely a formal pattern; at least one structure
satisfies them. This axiom guarantees that the abstract counting system is
available before it receives the conventional name $\mathbb{N}$.

\citet{FefermanNumberSystems1964}, where the existence of at least one Peano
system is taken as a foundational assumption.

support_blocks.body_tex:
For a Peano system $(P,S,1)$ and a predicate $\varphi$ on $P$,
\[
\Bigl(\varphi(1) \land
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n)))\Bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n).
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.] The named branch below records the contrapositive failure
  pattern for induction.
  \item[\(\operatorname{InductionPrinciple}\) fails.] The induction conclusion
  can fail only when the base case or the successor step fails:
  \[
  \neg\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n)
  \Longrightarrow
  \neg\Bigl(\varphi(1) \land
  \forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n)))\Bigr).
  \]
  In predicate-reading form this is recorded by the negation of
  \[
  \operatorname{InductionPrinciple}(P,S,1).
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } \varphi
\text{ be a predicate on } P.\\
&\neg\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n)
\Longrightarrow
\neg\Bigl(\varphi(1) \land
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n)))\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Contrapositive predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } (P,S,1) \text{ be a Peano system and let } \varphi
\text{ be a predicate on } P.\\
&\neg\forall n \in P\;\varphi(n)
\Longrightarrow
\neg\Bigl(\varphi(1) \land
\forall n \in P\;(\varphi(n) \Longrightarrow \varphi(S(n)))\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This theorem converts the subset form of induction into the predicate form
used in ordinary arithmetic arguments. A property propagates through the
entire Peano system once it holds at the distinguished first element and is
preserved by successor. The theorem therefore turns the structural induction
axiom into a proof principle for arbitrary predicates on $P$.

support_blocks.title: Source comparison
support_blocks.body_tex:
Peano's axiomatization includes induction as part of the natural-number
structure. Feferman derives the working form of mathematical induction from
the subset formulation of the Peano axioms immediately after Theorem 3.3 in
Chapter 3. The present notes formalize that induction principle as an explicit
reusable theorem. \citep{PeanoArithmeticesPrincipia1889}; \citet{FefermanNumberSystems1964}

nodes.name: Strong Induction on a Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $<$ be a binary relation on $P$, and let
$\varphi$ be a predicate on $P$. Suppose that $<$ is compatible with the
successor structure in the following sense:
\[
\forall k\in P,\qquad \neg(k<1),
\]
and
\[
\forall k,n\in P,\qquad
k<S(n)\Longleftrightarrow (k<n\lor k=n).
\]
If
\[
\forall n \in P,\qquad
\left[
\left(\forall k \in P,\ k < n \Longrightarrow \varphi(k)\right)
\Longrightarrow \varphi(n)
\right]
\]
then
\[
\forall n \in P,\qquad \varphi(n).
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
For a Peano system $(P,S,1)$, a binary relation $<$ on $P$, and a predicate
$\varphi$ on $P$,
\[
\Bigl[
\bigl(\forall k\in P,\ \neg(k<1)\bigr)
\land
\bigl(\forall k,n\in P,\ k<S(n)\Longleftrightarrow(k<n\lor k=n)\bigr)
\land\\
\qquad
\forall n \in P,\quad
\left(
\left(\forall k \in P,\ k < n \Longrightarrow \varphi(k)\right)
\Longrightarrow \varphi(n)
\right)
\Bigr]
\Longrightarrow
\forall n \in P,\ \varphi(n).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Strong induction grants the inductive step access to the entire history below
$n$, not just the single predecessor. It is the proof form behind least
counterexample arguments.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
A successor-closed subset is stable under one step of counting. Once an
element of $A$ is present, its successor remains in $A$ as well.

support_blocks.title: Source comparison
support_blocks.body_tex:
The notion of a successor-closed subset is implicit in condition (iii) of
Feferman's Definition 3.1. The present notes isolate it as a separate
definition so that induction arguments can refer to the closure condition
directly. \citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964}

nodes.name: Minimality of a Peano System
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system. If $A\subseteq P$ contains $1$ and is closed
under successor, then $A=P$. In quantified form,
\[
\forall A\subseteq P,\qquad
\left[
\left(1\in A \land
\forall n\in A,\ S(n)\in A\right)
\Longrightarrow A=P
\right]
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Every element of a Peano system is reached by starting at the distinguished
first element and moving forward by successor. The only possible exception to
having a predecessor is the element $1$ itself.

support_blocks.title: Historical note
support_blocks.body_tex:
This theorem is one of the basic successor consequences of Peano's
axiomatization \citep{PeanoArithmeticesPrincipia1889}. In the present
organization it corresponds directly to Theorem 3.3 in
\citet{FefermanNumberSystems1964}. Feferman uses this result to show that
the distinguished initial element is the only possible non-successor in a
Peano system.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Successor always moves forward in the counting structure. No element can be
recovered by applying successor to itself.

support_blocks.title: Historical note
support_blocks.body_tex:
This theorem is a standard consequence of the Peano axioms in the classical
development of the natural numbers \citep{PeanoArithmeticesPrincipia1889}.
Feferman includes the corresponding result as an exercise in Chapter 3 of
\citet{FefermanNumberSystems1964}.

examples.label: Why the base case is forced
examples.title: Why the base case is forced
examples.body_tex:
For the first element, the theorem says
\[
S(1)\neq 1.
\]
This is exactly the axiom that the distinguished element is not a successor:
there is no element $x\in P$ with $S(x)=1$. In particular, taking $x=1$
would be impossible, so $S(1)\neq 1$.

examples.label: Why the induction step uses injectivity
examples.title: Why the induction step uses injectivity
examples.body_tex:
Suppose the induction hypothesis gives $S(n)\neq n$. To prove the next case,
we must show
\[
S(S(n))\neq S(n).
\]
If equality held, injectivity of $S$ would let us cancel the outer successor
and conclude $S(n)=n$, contradicting the induction hypothesis. Thus the
property propagates from $n$ to $S(n)$.

nodes.name: Presburger Signature
nodes.statement_display:
The \emph{Presburger signature} is the first-order signature
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Pres}} = \{0, S, +, <\},
\]
where $0$ is a constant symbol, $S$ is a unary function symbol, $+$ is a
binary function symbol, and $<$ is a binary relation symbol. Equality is the
logical equality symbol of first-order logic, not an additional nonlogical
relation symbol of the signature.

support_blocks.body_tex:
The Presburger signature names addition and order, but it deliberately omits
multiplication as a function symbol. This makes Presburger arithmetic a theory
of the additive structure of the natural numbers rather than a theory of full
arithmetic.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Presburger arithmetic isolates the part of arithmetic governed by addition.
It is strong enough to express linear equations, congruences, and order
properties of natural numbers, but it cannot directly express multiplication
as a primitive operation. The later Peano-system material supplies the more
general recursive framework from which addition, multiplication, order, and
induction are developed structurally.

nodes.text_preview: Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $W$ be a set, let $c\in W$, and let $g:W\to W$ be a function. The triple $(W,c,g)$ is called \emph{iterator data} for $(P,S,1)$.

(W,c,g) \text{ is iterator data for } (P,S,1)
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(W \text{ is a set}\land c\in W\land g:W\to W\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading

\]

(W,c,g) \text{ is not iterator data for } (P,S,1)

\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Iterator data fails if the proposed value collection is not a set, if the
  initial value does not lie in the value set, or if the proposed update rule
  is not a self-map of the value set.
  \item[Invalid data.]
  \[
  \neg\operatorname{IteratorData}(W,c,g).
  \]
  \[
  \begin{aligned}
  &(W,c,g) \text{ is not iterator data for } (P,S,1)\\
  \Longleftrightarrow\;&
  \underbrace{W \text{ is not a set}}_{\text{no value set}}\\
  &\lor \underbrace{c\notin W}_{\text{invalid initial value}}\\
  &\lor \underbrace{g \text{ is not a function } W\to W}_{\text{invalid update rule}}.
  \end{aligned}
  \]
\end{description}

\[
(1,c)\in R
\]

\forall n\in P\;\forall w\in W\;
\bigl((n,w)\in R\Longrightarrow (S(n),g(w))\in R\bigr).
\]

nodes.name: Minimal Iterator Relation
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
The \emph{minimal iterator relation} for $(W,c,g)$ is
\[
R^*
=
\bigcap\{R\subseteq P\times W : R \text{ is an iterator relation for }
(W,c,g)\}.
\]

by the base pair and the successor closure rule. This is the $R^*$ construction
used in Feferman's proof of recursive definition, and in the related
set-theoretic presentations cited here
\citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964,hrbacek_jech1999,chi_recursion_wustl}.

$R^*$ be the minimal iterator relation. For each $n\in P$, there is at most one
$w\in W$ such that $(n,w)\in R^*$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Iterator Functions
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it. If
$f,h:P\to W$ satisfy
\[
f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=g(h(n))),
\]
then $f=h$.

nodes.name: Peano Iterator Theorem
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
Then there exists a unique function $f:P\to W$ such that
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n))).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The theorem says that iterator data is sufficient to turn a recursive
specification into a genuine definition: there is exactly one graph and hence
exactly one function satisfying the base and successor clauses.

support_blocks.title: Historical note
support_blocks.body_tex:
This is the one-based Peano-system version of the iterator theorem in
\citet{FefermanNumberSystems1964,MendelsonNumberSystemsFoundationsAnalysis,simpson2011peanosystems}.
It is also the set-theoretic instance of the natural numbers object universal
property \citep{lawvere1969adjointness}; Dedekind's recursion theorem is the
classical ancestor \citep{dedekind1901essays}.

nodes.name: Iterator-Generated Function
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, and let $(W,c,g)$ be iterator data for it.
The unique function $f:P\to W$ satisfying
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=g(f(n)))
\]
is called the \emph{iterator-generated function determined by $(W,c,g)$}.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Binary Iterator Operations
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $A$ be a set, let $W$ be a set, and
suppose each $a\in A$ determines iterator data $(W,c_a,g_a)$ for $(P,S,1)$.
If $F,G:A\times P\to W$ satisfy
\[
F(a,1)=c_a,\qquad G(a,1)=c_a
\]
and
\[
F(a,S(n))=g_a(F(a,n)),
\qquad
G(a,S(n))=g_a(G(a,n))
\]
for all $a\in A$ and all $n\in P$, then $F=G$.

existence is invoked \citep{thurston1956numbersystem}.

nodes.name: Solution of a Stage-Dependent Recursion
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $W$ be a set, let $c\in W$, and let
$\Phi\colon P\times W\to W$ be a stage-dependent step rule. A function
$f\colon P\to W$
is called a \emph{solution of the stage-dependent recursion determined by
$(W,c,\Phi)$}
exactly when
\[
f(1)=c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=\Phi(n,f(n))).
\]

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Stage-Dependent Recursion Solutions
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $W$ be a set, let $c\in W$, and let
$\Phi\colon P\times W\to W$ be a stage-dependent step rule. If
$f,h\colon P\to W$ satisfy
\[
f(1)=c,\qquad h(1)=c,
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(f(S(n))=\Phi(n,f(n)))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\forall n\in P\;(h(S(n))=\Phi(n,h(n))),
\]
then $f=h$.

nodes.name: General Recursion by State Encoding
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S,1)$ be a Peano system, let $W$ be a set, let $c\in W$, and let
$\Phi\colon P\times W\to W$ be a stage-dependent step rule. Define
\[
G\colon P\times W\to P\times W,
\qquad
(n,w)\mapsto (S(n),\Phi(n,w)).
\]
Then there exists a unique function $H\colon P\to P\times W$ such that
\[
H(1)=(1,c)
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P,\qquad
H(S(n))=G(H(n)).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\forall n\in P,\qquad
H(S(n))=
\left(S(\pi_1(H(n))),\Phi(\pi_1(H(n)),\pi_2(H(n)))\right).
\]

General recursion justifies recursive definitions whose successor rule depends
on the current stage as well as the current value. Definitions of addition,
multiplication, exponentiation, and later arithmetic operations are not part
of this section. They begin after the recursion principles have been
established.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Peano Systems up to Isomorphism
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,S_P,1_P)$ and $(Q,S_Q,1_Q)$ be Peano systems. Then there exists a
unique bijection $\theta:P\to Q$ such that
\[
\theta(1_P)=1_Q
\]
and
\[
\forall n\in P\;(\theta(S_P(n))=S_Q(\theta(n))).
\]
Thus any two Peano systems are isomorphic.

support_blocks.body_tex:
All Peano systems have the same structure up to a unique isomorphism. The
elements may be named differently, but the distinguished first element and
successor structure determine the translation.

This is the categoricity theorem for Peano systems, following Feferman's
Theorem 3.5 and Simpson's Peano-system presentation
\citep{FefermanNumberSystems1964,simpson2011peanosystems}.

\[
A\neq\varnothing,\quad A\text{ bounded above},\quad c\in\mathbb{R}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sup\{a+c:a\in A\}=\sup A+c.
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\qquad A\subseteq\mathbb{R},\qquad A+c=\{a+c:a\in A\},\\
&\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s+c,A+c,P).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\sup(A+c)\ne \sup A+c
\]
is impossible under the stated hypotheses.

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\qquad A\subseteq\mathbb{R},\qquad A+c=\{a+c:a\in A\},\\
&\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)\land
\neg\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s+c,A+c,P)
\end{aligned}
\]
is a contradictory configuration.

&\Longleftrightarrow
\forall v\,[\operatorname{UpperBound}(v,A+c)\Longrightarrow s+c\leq v].
\end{aligned}
\]

\sup(A+c)\ne \sup A+c
\]

\end{aligned}
\]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Translation Invariance of the Infimum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
$c\in\mathbb{R}$.  Then $A+c:=\{a+c:a\in A\}$ is nonempty and bounded below,
and
\[
  \inf(A+c)=\inf A+c.
\]

nodes.name: Scalar Multiplication by a Positive Scalar
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let
$k\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $k>0$.  Then $kA:=\{ka:a\in A\}$ is nonempty and
bounded above, and
\[
  \sup(kA)=k\sup A.
\]

nodes.name: Scalar Multiplication by a Negative Scalar
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
$k\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $k<0$.  Then $kA:=\{ka:a\in A\}$ is nonempty and
bounded above, and
\[
  \sup(kA)=k\inf A.
\]

nodes.source_text:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
$k\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $k<0$.  Then $kA:=\{ka:a\in A\}$ is nonempty and
bounded above, and
\[
  \sup(kA)=k\inf A.
\]

Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty, with $A$ bounded below and $B$
bounded above.  Then $A-B:=\{a-b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}$ is nonempty and bounded
below, and
\[
  \inf(A-B)=\inf A-\sup B.
\]

\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(t-s,A-B,P).

\]

nodes.name: Supremum of a Dilation
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$.  Then $\lambda A:=\{\lambda a:a\in A\}$ is nonempty
and bounded above, and
\[
  \sup(\lambda A)=
  \begin{cases}
    \lambda\sup A, & \lambda>0,\\
    0, & \lambda=0,\\
    \lambda\inf A, & \lambda<0.
  \end{cases}
\]

nodes.name: Supremum of a Reciprocal Set
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded, and suppose that
$0<\inf A$ or $\sup A<0$.  Define
\[
  A^{-1}:=\{1/a:a\in A\}.
\]
Then $A^{-1}$ is bounded above, and
\[
  \sup(A^{-1})=\frac{1}{\inf A}.
\]

nodes.name: Supremum of a Product Set
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded.  Then
$AB:=\{ab:a\in A,\ b\in B\}$ is bounded, and
\[
  \sup(AB)=
  \max\{(\inf A)(\inf B),(\inf A)(\sup B),(\sup A)(\inf B),(\sup A)(\sup B)\}.
\]

nodes.name: Supremum of a Quotient Set
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded, and suppose
$0<\inf B$ or $\sup B<0$.  Then
$A/B:=\{a/b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}$ is bounded, and
\[
  \sup(A/B)=
  \max\left\{\frac{\inf A}{\inf B},\frac{\inf A}{\sup B},
              \frac{\sup A}{\inf B},\frac{\sup A}{\sup B}\right\}.
\]

\]

nodes.name: Bounds for Suprema and Infima Under Set Addition
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, and let
$u_A,u_B,\ell_A,\ell_B\in\mathbb{R}$.  If $u_A$ is an upper bound of $A$ and
$u_B$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $u_A+u_B$ is an upper bound of $A+B$:
\[
  \left[(\forall a\in A)(a\leq u_A)\land
  (\forall b\in B)(b\leq u_B)\right]
  \Longrightarrow
  (\forall x\in A+B)(x\leq u_A+u_B).
\]
If $\ell_A$ is a lower bound of $A$ and $\ell_B$ is a lower bound of $B$, then
$\ell_A+\ell_B$ is a lower bound of $A+B$:
\[
  \left[(\forall a\in A)(\ell_A\leq a)\land
  (\forall b\in B)(\ell_B\leq b)\right]
  \Longrightarrow
  (\forall x\in A+B)(\ell_A+\ell_B\leq x).
\]

nodes.name: Upper Bounds Depend on the Ambient Order
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(P,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set, and let
$A\subseteq S\subseteq S'\subseteq P$.  The upper bounds of $A$ relative to
$S$ are exactly those upper bounds of $A$ relative to $S'$ that belong to $S$:
\[
  \{u\in S:(\forall a\in A)(a\leq u)\}
  =
  S\cap\{u\in S':(\forall a\in A)(a\leq u)\}.
\]

nodes.name: Suprema Depend on the Ambient Set
nodes.statement_display:
There exist a linearly ordered set $(P,\leq)$, subsets
$A\subseteq S\subseteq S'\subseteq P$, and relative suprema $\sup_S A$ and
$\sup_{S'}A$ such that
\[
  \sup_S A\ne\sup_{S'}A.
\]
For example, in $\mathbb{R}$, let
\[
  A=(0,1),\qquad
  S=(0,1)\cup\{2\},
  \qquad
  S'=(0,1)\cup\left\{\frac{3}{2},2\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
  \sup_S A=2,
  \qquad
  \sup_{S'}A=\frac{3}{2}.
\]

nodes.name: Ambient Existence of Supremum
nodes.statement_display:
There exist a linearly ordered set $(P,\leq)$ and subsets
$A\subseteq S\subseteq S'\subseteq P$ such that $A$ has a supremum relative to
$S'$ but has no supremum relative to $S$.  For example, in $\mathbb{R}$, let
\[
  A=S=(0,1),
  \qquad
  S'=(0,1].
\]
Then
\[
  \sup_{S'}A=1,
\]
whereas $A$ has no upper bound in $S$, and hence no supremum relative to $S$.

nodes.name: Rational Gap Example for Suprema
nodes.statement_display:
Let
\[
  A=\{q\in\mathbb{Q}:q^2<2\}.
\]
Then $A$ is nonempty and bounded above relative to $\mathbb{Q}$, but $A$ has
no supremum in $\mathbb{Q}$:
\[
  \nexists s\in\mathbb{Q}\left[
  (\forall q\in A)(q\leq s)
  \land
  \forall u\in\mathbb{Q}
  \bigl((\forall q\in A)(q\leq u)\Longrightarrow s\leq u\bigr)
  \right].
\]
When $A$ is regarded as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, its supremum exists and is
\[
  \sup_{\mathbb{R}}A=\sqrt{2}.
\]

nodes.name: Displacement, Dilation, and Reflection
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. For $c,\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$, the
\textbf{displacement} of $A$ by $c$, the \textbf{dilation} of $A$ by
$\lambda$, and the \textbf{reflection} of $A$ through the origin are
defined, respectively, by
\[
A+c:=\{a+c:a\in A\},
\qquad
\lambda A:=\{\lambda a:a\in A\},
\qquad
-A:=\{-a:a\in A\}.
\]

\operatorname{ReplacementImage}(\lambda A,A,\varphi_\lambda),\qquad

\end{aligned}
\]

upper bound of $A$, then $u+c$ is an upper bound of $A+c$; that is,
\[
\left(\forall a\in A,\ a\leq u\right)
\Longrightarrow
\left(\forall x\in A+c,\ x\leq u+c\right).
\]

nodes.name: Reflection Swaps Upper and Lower Bounds
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. For every $b\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
b\text{ is an upper bound of }A
\Longleftrightarrow
-b\text{ is a lower bound of }-A,
\]
and
\[
b\text{ is a lower bound of }A
\Longleftrightarrow
-b\text{ is an upper bound of }-A.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\left(\forall a\in A,\ a\leq b\right)
\Longleftrightarrow
\left(\forall x\in -A,\ -b\leq x\right),
\]
and
\[
\left(\forall a\in A,\ b\leq a\right)
\Longleftrightarrow
\left(\forall x\in -A,\ x\leq -b\right).
\]

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $A\subseteq I$ be nonempty and
bounded above, and suppose $s:=\sup A\in I$.  If $f\colon I\to\mathbb{R}$ is
increasing and continuous at $s$ relative to $I$, then
$f[A]:=\{f(a):a\in A\}$ is bounded above, and
\[
  \sup f[A]=f(\sup A).
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
A\neq\varnothing,\quad s=\sup A\in I,\quad f\text{ increasing and continuous at }s
\Longrightarrow
\sup\{f(a):a\in A\}=f(s).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&A\subseteq I,\qquad f\colon I\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
B=f(A)=\{f(a):a\in A\},\\
&P_I=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(I,\leq),\qquad
P_{\mathbb{R}}=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\\
&\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P_I)\land
\operatorname{OrderPreserving}(f,P_I,P_{\mathbb{R}})\land
\operatorname{IsContinuous}(f,s,I,\mathbb{R})
\Longrightarrow
\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(f(s),B,P_{\mathbb{R}}).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\sup f(A)\neq f(\sup A)
\]
is impossible under the stated hypotheses.

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&A\subseteq I,\qquad f\colon I\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
B=f(A)=\{f(a):a\in A\},\\
&P_I=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(I,\leq),\qquad
P_{\mathbb{R}}=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\\
&\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P_I)\land
\operatorname{OrderPreserving}(f,P_I,P_{\mathbb{R}})\land
\operatorname{IsContinuous}(f,s,I,\mathbb{R})\land
\neg\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(f(s),B,P_{\mathbb{R}}).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
\item[Exposition.]
Increasingness gives $f(a)\leq f(s)$ for every $a\in A$.  The defining
approximation property of the supremum gives points of $A$ arbitrarily close
to $s$ from below, and continuity at $s$ makes their images approach $f(s)$.


  \item[\(\operatorname{LeastUpperBound} / \operatorname{OrderPreserving}.\)]
  \[
\sup f(A)\neq f(\sup A)
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
&A\subseteq I,\qquad f\colon I\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
B=f(A)=\{f(a):a\in A\},\\
&P_I=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(I,\leq),\qquad
P_{\mathbb{R}}=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\\
&\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P_I)\land
\operatorname{OrderPreserving}(f,P_I,P_{\mathbb{R}})\land
\operatorname{IsContinuous}(f,s,I,\mathbb{R})\land
\neg\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(f(s),B,P_{\mathbb{R}}).
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Decreasing Inverse Sends Infimum to Supremum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $I,J\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be intervals, and let $f\colon I\to J$ be a continuous
strictly decreasing bijection.  Let $B\subseteq J$ be nonempty and bounded
below, and suppose $\inf B\in J$.  Then
$f^{-1}[B]:=\{f^{-1}(b):b\in B\}$ is bounded above, and
\[
  \sup f^{-1}[B]=f^{-1}(\inf B).
\]

nodes.name: Pairwise Maximum and Minimum Sets
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$.  The \emph{pairwise maximum set} and
\emph{pairwise minimum set} of $A$ and $B$ are defined, respectively, by
\[
  A\vee B:=\{\max\{a,b\}:a\in A,\ b\in B\},
\]
and
\[
  A\wedge B:=\{\min\{a,b\}:a\in A,\ b\in B\}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
x\in A\vee B
\Longleftrightarrow
(\exists a\in A)(\exists b\in B)\bigl(x=\max\{a,b\}\bigr),
\]
and
\[
x\in A\wedge B
\Longleftrightarrow
(\exists a\in A)(\exists b\in B)\bigl(x=\min\{a,b\}\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R},\qquad D=A\times B,\\
&M=A\vee B=\{\max\{a,b\}:a\in A,\ b\in B\},\\
&N=A\wedge B=\{\min\{a,b\}:a\in A,\ b\in B\},\\
&\varphi_{\max}\colon D\to M,\qquad \varphi_{\min}\colon D\to N,\\
&\varphi_{\max}(a,b)=\max\{a,b\},\qquad
\varphi_{\min}(a,b)=\min\{a,b\},\\
&\operatorname{ReplacementImage}(M,D,\varphi_{\max}),\qquad
\operatorname{ReplacementImage}(N,D,\varphi_{\min}).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
x\notin A\vee B
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall a\in A)(\forall b\in B)\bigl(x\neq\max\{a,b\}\bigr),
\]
and
\[
x\notin A\wedge B
\Longleftrightarrow
(\forall a\in A)(\forall b\in B)\bigl(x\neq\min\{a,b\}\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:

\begin{aligned}

M=A\vee B=\{\max\{a,b\}:a\in A,\ b\in B\},\\
&C\ne M
\end{aligned}
\quad\text{means}\quad
(\exists x)\bigl[x\in C\triangle M\bigr],
\]

nodes.name: Union Preserves Upper Bounds
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. For every $u\in\mathbb{R}$, if $u$ is an
upper bound of both $A$ and $B$, then $u$ is an upper bound of
$A\cup B$; that is,
\[
\left[
(\forall a\in A,\ a\leq u)
\land
(\forall b\in B,\ b\leq u)
\right]
\Longrightarrow
(\forall x\in A\cup B,\ x\leq u).
\]

lower-bound hypothesis gives $\ell\leq x$.

nodes.name: Union Is Bounded Above Exactly When Both Pieces Are
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. The union $A\cup B$ is bounded above if and
only if both $A$ and $B$ are bounded above; equivalently,
\[
\left(\exists u\in\mathbb{R}\ \forall x\in A\cup B,\ x\leq u\right)
\Longleftrightarrow
\left[
\left(\exists u_A\in\mathbb{R}\ \forall a\in A,\ a\leq u_A\right)
\land
\left(\exists u_B\in\mathbb{R}\ \forall b\in B,\ b\leq u_B\right)
\right].
\]

nodes.name: Union Is Bounded Exactly When Both Pieces Are
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. The union $A\cup B$ is bounded if and only
if both $A$ and $B$ are bounded; that is,
\[
A\cup B\text{ is bounded}
\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(A\text{ is bounded}\land B\text{ is bounded}\bigr).
\]

nodes.name: Subsets Preserve Upper Bounds
nodes.statement_display:
Let $C\subseteq A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. Every upper bound of $A$ is an
upper bound of $C$; that is, for every $u\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\left(\forall a\in A,\ a\leq u\right)
\Longrightarrow
(\forall c\in C,\ c\leq u).
\]
Consequently, every subset of a set bounded above is bounded above.

nodes.name: Intersections Inherit Bounds
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. Every upper bound of $A$ or of $B$ is an
upper bound of $A\cap B$, and every lower bound of $A$ or of $B$ is a
lower bound of $A\cap B$; that is, for all $u,\ell\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
\left[
(\forall a\in A,\ a\leq u)
\lor
(\forall b\in B,\ b\leq u)
\right]
\Longrightarrow
(\forall x\in A\cap B,\ x\leq u),
\]
and
\[
\left[
(\forall a\in A,\ \ell\leq a)
\lor
(\forall b\in B,\ \ell\leq b)
\right]
\Longrightarrow
(\forall x\in A\cap B,\ \ell\leq x).
\]

nodes.name: Epsilon Characterization of the Supremum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let
$s\in\mathbb{R}$. Then
\[
  s=\sup A
\]
if and only if both of the following conditions hold:
\[
  (\forall a\in A)(a\leq s),
\]
and
\[
  (\forall\varepsilon>0)(\exists a\in A)(s-\varepsilon<a).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  s=\sup A
  \Longleftrightarrow
  \left[
    (\forall a\in A)(a\leq s)
    \land
    (\forall\varepsilon>0)(\exists a\in A)(s-\varepsilon<a\leq s)
  \right].
\]

nodes.name: Epsilon Characterization of the Infimum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
$i\in\mathbb{R}$. Then
\[
  i=\inf A
\]
if and only if both of the following conditions hold:
\[
  (\forall a\in A)(i\leq a),
\]
and
\[
  (\forall\varepsilon>0)(\exists a\in A)(a<i+\varepsilon).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  i=\inf A
  \Longleftrightarrow
  \left[
    (\forall a\in A)(i\leq a)
    \land
    (\forall\varepsilon>0)(\exists a\in A)(i\leq a<i+\varepsilon)
  \right].
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This condition says that $i$ sits below the set while points of $A$ approach $i$ from above at every positive scale. The lower-bound clause prevents $A$ from crossing below $i$, and the epsilon clause prevents $i$ from sitting strictly below the set with a positive gap. Geometrically, $i$ is a floor that the set presses against arbitrarily closely from above.


The epsilon characterizations are one way to prove the sharpness part of a
supremum or infimum claim.  After proving the candidate is an upper or lower
bound, one can either compare it with arbitrary bounds directly or build
near-extremal points using an arbitrary $\varepsilon>0$.  The proof-techniques
chapter gives a fuller guide to choosing between these approaches:
\hyperref[subsec:eps-char]{The $\varepsilon$-Characterisation of Suprema and
Infima}.

nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
$i=\inf A$.  For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$ with $i<x$, there exists
$a\in A$ such that
\[
i\le a<x.
\]

nodes.name: Maximum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ and let $m\in\mathbb{R}$. The number $m$ is the
\emph{maximum} of $A$, written $m=\max A$, if
\[
  m\in A
  \land
  (\forall a\in A)(a\leq m).
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Maximum failure means the candidate is not an attained upper bound of
  the set.

  \item[\(\operatorname{GreatestElement}.\)]
  The candidate is not an element of the set.
  \[
    m\notin A.
  \]
  \[
    P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\qquad
    \neg\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P).
  \]

  \item[\(\operatorname{UpperBound}.\)]
  Some element of the set lies strictly above the candidate.
  \[
    (\exists a\in A)(m<a).
  \]
  \[
    P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\qquad
    \neg\operatorname{UpperBound}(m,A,P).
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the Maximum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. If $m_1,m_2\in\mathbb{R}$ are both maxima of
$A$, then
\[
  m_1=m_2.
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  \operatorname{GreatestElement}(m_{1},A,P)
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \operatorname{GreatestElement}(m_{2},A,P)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  m_{1}=m_{2}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  A\subseteq\mathbb{R},\qquad P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\qquad
  \operatorname{GreatestElement}(m_{1},A,P)\land
  \operatorname{GreatestElement}(m_{2},A,P)
  \Longrightarrow m_{1}=m_{2}.
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:

  \quad\text{and}\quad

  \quad\text{and}\quad
  m_{1}\neq m_{2}.
\]

  A\subseteq\mathbb{R},\qquad P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\qquad
  \operatorname{GreatestElement}(m_{1},A,P)\land
  \operatorname{GreatestElement}(m_{2},A,P)\land m_{1}\neq m_{2}.
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Failure would require two distinct elements of $A$ each to dominate the
  entire set.

  \item[\(\operatorname{GreatestElement}.\)]
  Two different candidates both satisfy the maximum predicate.
  \[
    \operatorname{GreatestElement}(m_{1},A,P)\land
    \operatorname{GreatestElement}(m_{2},A,P)\land m_{1}\neq m_{2}.
  \]
  \[
    P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\qquad
    \operatorname{GreatestElement}(m_{1},A,P)\land
    \operatorname{GreatestElement}(m_{2},A,P)\land m_{1}\neq m_{2}.
  \]
\end{description}

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
$i=\inf A$. If $i\in A$, then
\[
  i=\min A.
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:

\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Failure would require an infimum that belongs to the set but is not its
  minimum.

  \item[\(\operatorname{GreatestLowerBound} / \operatorname{LeastElement}.\)]
  The candidate is a greatest lower bound, belongs to the set, and yet is not
  the least element.
  \[
    \operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(i,A,P)\land i\in A\land
    \neg\operatorname{LeastElement}(i,A,P).
  \]
  \[
    P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\qquad
    \operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(i,A,P)\land i\in A\land
    \neg\operatorname{LeastElement}(i,A,P).
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: A Set Has a Maximum If and Only If Its Supremum Belongs to the Set
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let $s=\sup A$.
Then
\[
  A\text{ has a maximum}
  \Longleftrightarrow
  s\in A,
\]
and when this holds, $\max A = s$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  A\neq\varnothing,\quad\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  \bigl[(\exists m\in\mathbb{R})\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)
  \Longleftrightarrow s\in A\bigr].
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\qquad A\subseteq\mathbb{R},\qquad
  A\neq\varnothing\land\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \Longrightarrow
  \bigl[(\exists m)\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\leftrightarrow s\in A\bigr].
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  A\neq\varnothing,\quad\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P),
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \bigl[(\exists m\in\mathbb{R})\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\land s\notin A\bigr]
  \ \text{or}\
  \bigl[s\in A\land(\forall m\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\bigr].
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Failure would mean a maximum exists while the supremum lies outside the
  set, or the supremum lies in the set while no maximum exists.

  
\[
A\neq\varnothing,\quad\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P),
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \bigl[(\exists m\in\mathbb{R})\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\land s\notin A\bigr]
  \ \text{or}\
  \bigl[s\in A\land(\forall m\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\bigr].
\]

\[
A\neq\varnothing,\quad\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P),
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \bigl[(\exists m\in\mathbb{R})\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\land s\notin A\bigr]
  \ \text{or}\
  \bigl[s\in A\land(\forall m\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\bigr].
\]
  \item[\(\operatorname{GreatestElement} / \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}.\)]
\[
A\neq\varnothing,\quad\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P),
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \bigl[(\exists m\in\mathbb{R})\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\land s\notin A\bigr]
  \ \text{or}\
  \bigl[s\in A\land(\forall m\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\bigr].
\]

\[
A\neq\varnothing,\quad\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P),
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \bigl[(\exists m\in\mathbb{R})\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\land s\notin A\bigr]
  \ \text{or}\
  \bigl[s\in A\land(\forall m\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{GreatestElement}(m,A,P)\bigr].
\]
  The forward direction combines \hyperref[prop:maximum-implies-supremum]{Maximum
  Implies Supremum} with \hyperref[prop:uniqueness-of-the-supremum]{Uniqueness
  of the Supremum}: any maximum is a supremum, and suprema are unique, so it
  must equal $s$ and hence $s\in A$. The reverse direction is
  \hyperref[prop:supremum-in-the-set-is-the-maximum]{Supremum in the Set Is
  the Maximum}.
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This packages the two one-directional propositions above into a single
if-and-only-if: ``attained'' and ``supremum'' coincide exactly at set
membership. It is worth stating as its own corollary because later
arguments often need to move freely in either direction (e.g. showing a
maximum exists by exhibiting the supremum inside the set, or ruling out a
maximum by showing the supremum lies outside it) rather than reaching for
the one-directional propositions and re-deriving the missing half by hand.

nodes.name: Relative Bounds
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(T,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq T$, and let $S\subseteq T$.
An element $u\in S$ is a \emph{relative upper bound of $A$ in $S$} if
\[
  (\forall a\in A)(a\leq u).
\]
An element $\ell\in S$ is a \emph{relative lower bound of $A$ in $S$} if
\[
  (\forall a\in A)(\ell\leq a).
\]

nodes.name: Relative Supremum and Infimum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(T,\leq)$ be an ordered set, let $A\subseteq T$, and let $S\subseteq T$.
An element $s\in S$ is the \emph{relative supremum of $A$ in $S$} if $s$ is a
relative upper bound of $A$ in $S$ and
\[
  (\forall u\in S)\left[
    (\forall a\in A)(a\leq u)\Longrightarrow s\leq u
  \right].
\]
An element $i\in S$ is the \emph{relative infimum of $A$ in $S$} if $i$ is a
relative lower bound of $A$ in $S$ and
\[
  (\forall \ell\in S)\left[
    (\forall a\in A)(\ell\leq a)\Longrightarrow \ell\leq i
  \right].
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  s\in S\land(\forall a\in A)(a\leq s)\land
  (\forall u\in S)\left[
    (\forall a\in A)(a\leq u)\Longrightarrow s\leq u
  \right],
\]
\[
  i\in S\land(\forall a\in A)(i\leq a)\land
  (\forall \ell\in S)\left[
    (\forall a\in A)(\ell\leq a)\Longrightarrow \ell\leq i
  \right].
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
  P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(T,\leq),\qquad A\subseteq T,\qquad S\subseteq T,
\]
\[
  \mathsf{RelativeSupremum}(s,A,S,P)
  :=
  \mathsf{RelativeUpperBound}(s,A,S,P)
  \land
  (\forall u\in S)
  \bigl(\mathsf{RelativeUpperBound}(u,A,S,P)\Rightarrow s\leq u\bigr),
\]
\[
  \mathsf{RelativeInfimum}(i,A,S,P)
  :=
  \mathsf{RelativeLowerBound}(i,A,S,P)
  \land
  (\forall \ell\in S)
  \bigl(\mathsf{RelativeLowerBound}(\ell,A,S,P)\Rightarrow \ell\leq i\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Relative suprema and infima are sharp bounds after restricting the allowed
bound candidates to the ambient carrier $S$.
By default, the ambient set $S$ is assumed to contain the set under discussion:
$A\subseteq S$.  The definitions above can still be stated syntactically with
an arbitrary ambient set $S\subseteq T$ when it is useful to isolate which
candidates are allowed to serve as bounds.

The same ordered data can have different sharp bounds depending on the
ambient carrier.  For example,
\[
  A=\{q\in\mathbb{Q}:q^2<2\}
\]
has no relative supremum in $\mathbb{Q}$, but it has supremum $\sqrt{2}$ when
viewed as a subset of $\mathbb{R}$.  This is not a contradiction: the allowed
upper bounds changed from rational candidates to real candidates.

nodes.name: Rational Square-Less-Than-Two Set in the Reals
nodes.statement_display:
Let
\[
  R_{<\sqrt2}:=\{x\in\mathbb R:(\exists q\in\mathbb Q)\, x=q \text{ and } q^2<2\}.
\]
This is the set of rationals whose square is less than $2$, viewed as a subset of $\mathbb R$.

nodes.name: Supremum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$, and let
$s\in S$. The element $s$ is the \emph{supremum} of $A$, written
$s=\sup A$, if
\[
  (\forall a\in A)(a\leq s)
\]
and
\[
  (\forall u\in S)
  \left[
    (\forall a\in A)(a\leq u)
    \Longrightarrow
    s\leq u
  \right].
\]
Thus, $s$ is the least upper bound of $A$ in $S$.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  The set may be empty; $s$ may fail to be an upper bound; or $s$ may be an
  upper bound that is not least among upper bounds.

  \item[\(\operatorname{LeastUpperBound} / \operatorname{UpperBound}.\)]
  The first clause is a domain failure.  The second is a bound failure.  The
  third is a sharpness failure witnessed by a strictly smaller upper bound.
  \[
    A=\varnothing
    \quad\text{or}\quad
    (\exists a\in A)(s<a)
    \quad\text{or}\quad
    (\exists u\in\mathbb{R})\bigl[(\forall a\in A)(a\leq u)\ \text{and}\ u<s\bigr].
  \]
  \[
    \neg\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
    \Longleftrightarrow
    A=\varnothing
    \lor
    \neg\operatorname{UpperBound}(s,A,P)
    \lor
    (\exists u\in\mathbb{R})
    \bigl(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P)\land u<s\bigr).
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Exposition
support_blocks.body_tex:
Nonemptiness is a standing hypothesis for real suprema in this section.  The
empty set is bounded above in $\mathbb{R}$, but it has no real supremum:
every real number is an upper bound of $\varnothing$, and $\mathbb{R}$ has no
least element.

Let $(S,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$, and suppose
that $s=\sup A$ exists in $S$. Then $s$ is an upper bound of $A$; that is,
\[

nodes.name: Subset Inclusion Preserves Upper Bounds
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set, let $A,B\subseteq S$, and suppose
that $A\subseteq B$. If $u\in S$ is an upper bound of $B$, then $u$ is an
upper bound of $A$; equivalently,
\[
  \left[(\forall b\in B)(b\leq u)\right]
  \Longrightarrow
  \left[(\forall a\in A)(a\leq u)\right].
\]

  already works on the larger set.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Failure would mean enlarging a nonempty set lowers its least upper bound.

  
\[
A\subseteq B,\quad \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s_A,A,P),\quad
  \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s_B,B,P),\quad s_B<s_A.
\]
  \item[\(\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}.\)]
  The value $\sup B$ bounds $B$, hence bounds $A$; since $\sup A$ is least
  among upper bounds of $A$, $\sup A\leq\sup B$.
  \[
    A\subseteq B,\quad \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s_A,A,P),\quad
    \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s_B,B,P),\quad s_B<s_A.
  \]

nodes.name: Upper-Bound Comparison with the Supremum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above, and let
$s=\sup A$. For every $u\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
  u\text{ is an upper bound of }A
  \Longleftrightarrow
  s\leq u.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  (\forall a\in A)(a\leq u)
  \Longleftrightarrow
  s\leq u.
\]

\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Failure would mean an upper bound below the supremum, or a number above
  the supremum that fails to bound the set.

  
\[
\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  (\exists u)\bigl[(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P)\land u<s)
  \lor(s\leq u\land\neg\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P))\bigr].
\]
  \item[\(\operatorname{LeastUpperBound} / \operatorname{UpperBound}.\)]
  Leastness gives the forward implication.  The fact that $s$ bounds $A$
  gives the reverse implication by transitivity.
  \[
    \operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    (\exists u)\bigl[(\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P)\land u<s)
    \lor(s\leq u\land\neg\operatorname{UpperBound}(u,A,P))\bigr].
  \]

\end{description}

nodes.name: Lower-Bound Comparison with the Infimum
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below, and let
$i=\inf A$. For every $\ell\in\mathbb{R}$,
\[
  \ell\text{ is a lower bound of }A
  \Longleftrightarrow
  \ell\leq i.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  (\forall a\in A)(\ell\leq a)
  \Longleftrightarrow
  \ell\leq i.
\]

nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded above. Then there
exists a unique $s\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
  s=\sup A.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  (\forall A\subseteq\mathbb{R})
  \left[
    A\neq\varnothing
    \land
    (\exists u\in\mathbb{R})(\forall a\in A)(a\leq u)
    \Longrightarrow
    (\exists!s\in\mathbb{R})(s=\sup A)
  \right].
\]

nodes.name: Greatest-Lower-Bound Property Implies Existence of Infima
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ be nonempty and bounded below. Then there
exists a unique $i\in\mathbb{R}$ such that
\[
  i=\inf A.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
  (\forall A\subseteq\mathbb{R})
  \left[
    A\neq\varnothing
    \land
    (\exists \ell\in\mathbb{R})(\forall a\in A)(\ell\leq a)
    \Longrightarrow
    (\exists!i\in\mathbb{R})(i=\inf A)
  \right].
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
\[
  \mathbb{R}
\]
  In $\mathbb{R}$, neither existence clause can fail once the set is
  nonempty and bounded on the relevant side; this corollary simply records
  that both hold simultaneously when the set is bounded on both sides.

  
\[
A\neq\varnothing,\quad \operatorname{Bounded}(A,P),
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \bigl[(\forall s\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \ \text{or}\
  (\forall i\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(i,A,P)\bigr].
\]
  \item[\(\operatorname{LeastUpperBound} / \operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}.\)]
\[
A\neq\varnothing,\quad \operatorname{Bounded}(A,P),
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \bigl[(\forall s\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \ \text{or}\
  (\forall i\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(i,A,P)\bigr].
\]

\[
A\neq\varnothing,\quad \operatorname{Bounded}(A,P),
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  \bigl[(\forall s\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{LeastUpperBound}(s,A,P)
  \ \text{or}\
  (\forall i\in\mathbb{R})\neg\operatorname{GreatestLowerBound}(i,A,P)\bigr].
\]
  Apply \hyperref[thm:lub-property-implies-existence-of-suprema]{Least Upper
  Bound Property Implies Existence of Suprema} to the upper-bound half of
  $\operatorname{Bounded}(A,P)$, and
  \hyperref[thm:glb-property-implies-existence-of-infima]{Greatest Lower
  Bound Property Implies Existence of Infima} to the lower-bound half.
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
This is nothing more than the two existence theorems applied side by side:
a set that is bounded on both sides is exactly a set for which both the
supremum and the infimum are guaranteed to exist, each uniquely. It is
stated separately here because ``bounded'' (both-sided) is the hypothesis
that shows up constantly in later chapters, and it is worth having the
combined conclusion on hand as its own citable result rather than
re-deriving it from the two one-sided theorems every time.

nodes.name: Bound
nodes.statement_display:
Let $(S,\leq)$ be a partially ordered set, let $A\subseteq S$, and let
$b\in S$. The element $b$ is a \emph{bound} of $A$ if it is either an
upper bound or a lower bound of $A$; equivalently,
\[
  \bigl[(\forall a\in A)(a\leq b)\bigr]
  \lor
  \bigl[(\forall a\in A)(b\leq a)\bigr].
\]

    \land

If $A=\varnothing$, then every $b\in S$ is both an upper bound and a lower
bound of $A$, because the universal statements over $A$ are vacuously true.
This is intentional: nonemptiness is not part of being a bound.

\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
  Bounded-below failure means there is no single element of the ambient
  ordered set that lies below all elements of $A$.

  \item[\(\operatorname{BoundedBelow}.\)]
  Every proposed lower-bound candidate is defeated by a smaller element of $A$.
  \[
    (\forall \ell\in\mathbb{R})(\exists a\in A)(a<\ell).
  \]
  \[
    P=\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq),\qquad
    \neg\operatorname{BoundedBelow}(A,P).
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Bounded Set
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. The set $A$ is \emph{bounded} if it is bounded
above and bounded below; equivalently,
\[
  (\exists \ell,u\in\mathbb{R})(\forall a\in A)(\ell\leq a\leq u).
\]
Equivalently, $A$ is bounded if
\[
  (\exists M\geq 0)(\forall a\in A)(|a|\leq M).
\]

nodes.name: Bounded Set Is Equivalent to an Absolute-Value Bound
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$. Then $A$ is bounded if and only if there exists
$M\geq 0$ such that
\[
  (\forall a\in A)(|a|\leq M).
\]
