nodes.name: Refinement
nodes.statement_display: Let $[a,b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $P$ and $Q$ be partitions of $[a,b]$. Then $Q$ is a refinement of $P$ if and only if every point of $P$ is also a point of $Q$; equivalently, $P \subseteq Q$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Refinement formalizes the idea of subdividing an interval more finely without losing any previously chosen partition points. The condition $P \subseteq Q$ guarantees that every subinterval defined by $P$ is still represented when one passes to $Q$, allowing comparisons of sums or integrals computed on different meshes. Failure means that $Q$ discards at least one point of $P$, so information tied to that breakpoint would be lost when transitioning between partitions.

nodes.name: Common Refinement
nodes.statement_display: Let $a<b$ and let $P$ and $Q$ be partitions of $[a,b]$. Their common refinement is the partition $R$ obtained by taking the union of their node sets, so $R = P \cup Q$ as sets of points in $[a,b]$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\operatorname{IsCommonRefinement}(R,P,Q) \coloneqq (R = P \cup Q).
\]

support_blocks.title: Negated quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&a<b\land P,Q\subseteq [a,b]\land R\subseteq [a,b]\\
&\Longrightarrow
\neg\bigl(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}\;(x\in R\Longleftrightarrow x\in P\cup Q)\bigr)\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(\exists x\in R\;(x\notin P\cup Q)\bigr)
\lor
\bigl(\exists x\in P\cup Q\;(x\notin R)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\neg \operatorname{IsCommonRefinement}(R,P,Q) \Longleftrightarrow R \ne P \cup Q.
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
The claim that a partition $R$ is the common refinement of $P$ and $Q$ fails exactly when $R$ either contains a node not present in $P \cup Q$ or omits a node that $P \cup Q$ contributes. These are the only two structural ways in which $R$ can differ from $P \cup Q$.


  \item[\(\operatorname{IsCommonRefinement}.\)]
  The displayed obstruction is the corresponding failure mode.
  \[
\begin{aligned}
&a<b\land P,Q\subseteq [a,b]\land R\subseteq [a,b]\\
&\Longrightarrow
\neg\bigl(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}\;(x\in R\Longleftrightarrow x\in P\cup Q)\bigr)\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(\exists x\in R\;(x\notin P\cup Q)\bigr)
\lor
\bigl(\exists x\in P\cup Q\;(x\notin R)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
  \]
  \[
\neg \operatorname{IsCommonRefinement}(R,P,Q) \Longleftrightarrow R \ne P \cup Q.
  \]
\end{description}

\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
\[
R \ne P \cup Q
\Longleftrightarrow
\underbrace{\exists x \in R \setminus (P \cup Q)}_{\text{extra node}}
\;\lor\;
\underbrace{\exists x \in (P \cup Q) \setminus R}_{\text{missing node}}.
\]


  \item[\(\operatorname{IsCommonRefinement}.\)]
  The displayed obstruction is the corresponding failure mode.
  \[
\begin{aligned}
&a<b\land P,Q\subseteq [a,b]\land R\subseteq [a,b]\\
&\Longrightarrow
\neg\bigl(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}\;(x\in R\Longleftrightarrow x\in P\cup Q)\bigr)\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(\exists x\in R\;(x\notin P\cup Q)\bigr)
\lor
\bigl(\exists x\in P\cup Q\;(x\notin R)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
  \]
  \[
\neg \operatorname{IsCommonRefinement}(R,P,Q) \Longleftrightarrow R \ne P \cup Q.
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Forming the common refinement of two partitions simply collects every partition point that either partition already uses, producing the unique partition whose nodes are exactly those existing ones. No new nodes are created beyond those already in P or Q, and none are discarded; the construction merely merges the lists so that later comparisons, such as evaluating tagged sums on both partitions simultaneously, can be performed without further adjustment.

logical_blocks.failure_modes:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
The claim that a partition $R$ is the common refinement of $P$ and $Q$ fails exactly when $R$ either contains a node not present in $P \cup Q$ or omits a node that $P \cup Q$ contributes. These are the only two structural ways in which $R$ can differ from $P \cup Q$.


  \item[\(\operatorname{IsCommonRefinement}.\)]
  The displayed obstruction is the corresponding failure mode.
  \[
\begin{aligned}
&a<b\land P,Q\subseteq [a,b]\land R\subseteq [a,b]\\
&\Longrightarrow
\neg\bigl(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}\;(x\in R\Longleftrightarrow x\in P\cup Q)\bigr)\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\bigl(\exists x\in R\;(x\notin P\cup Q)\bigr)
\lor
\bigl(\exists x\in P\cup Q\;(x\notin R)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
  \]
  \[
\neg \operatorname{IsCommonRefinement}(R,P,Q) \Longleftrightarrow R \ne P \cup Q.
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Bounded on a Set
nodes.statement_display: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $f \colon A \to \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is bounded on $A$ if and only if there exists a constant $M>0$ such that $|f(x)| \le M$ for every $x \in A$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ and } f \colon A \to \mathbb{R}.\\
&f \text{ is bounded on } A
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists M>0 \; \forall x \in A \; (|f(x)| \le M).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  f\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\\
\operatorname{Bounded}(f,A) \coloneqq \exists M>0 \; \forall x \in A \; (|f(x)| \le M).
\end{aligned}
\]


\[
\operatorname{IsContinuous}(f,[a,b],\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})
\land \forall x\in[a,b]\;(f(x)\neq c)
\Longrightarrow
\Bigl[\bigl(\forall x\in[a,b]\; f(x)>c\bigr)
\lor
\bigl(\forall x\in[a,b]\; f(x)<c\bigr)\Bigr].
\]

\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The definition packages the informal idea that the values of $f$ stay within a fixed vertical strip over $A$. The witness $M$ serves as a uniform ceiling for the magnitudes $|f(x)|$, so once such an $M$ is known the graph of $f$ never escapes the band $[-M,M]$. Failure means that the outputs of $f$ grow without limit along some sequence of points inside $A$, so no finite strip can contain the entire image. Boundedness on a set is the foundational regularity hypothesis that underlies the boundedness and extreme value theorems for continuous functions on compact domains.

nodes.name: Boundedness Theorem
nodes.statement_display: Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$. Then there exists $M>0$ such that $|f(x)|\le M$ for every $x\in[a,b]$.

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } a<b \text{ and } f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}.\\
&\Bigl(\forall c\in[a,b]\;\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta>0\;\forall x\in[a,b]\bigl(|x-c|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon\bigr)\Bigr)\\
&\qquad\Longrightarrow \exists M>0\;\forall x\in[a,b]\;(|f(x)|\le M).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Negation predicate reading
Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
Each component hypothesis is indispensable: without closedness (for instance $f(x)=1/x$ on $(0,1]$) continuity does not prevent divergence near the missing endpoint; without bounded domain (for example $f(x)=x$ on $[0,\infty)$) linear growth forces unbounded values; without continuity (take $f(0)=0$ and $f(x)=1/x$ for $x\in(0,1]$) the discontinuity at $0$ again creates arbitrarily large magnitudes.


  \item[\(\operatorname{IsContinuous}.\)]
  The displayed obstruction is the corresponding failure mode.
  \[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } a<b \text{ and } f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}.\\
&\Bigl(\forall c\in[a,b]\;\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta>0\;\forall x\in[a,b]\bigl(|x-c|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon\bigr)\Bigr)\\
&\qquad\land \Bigl(\forall M>0\;\exists x\in[a,b]\;(|f(x)|>M)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
  \]
  \[
\operatorname{IsContinuous}(f,[a,b],\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) \land \neg\operatorname{Bounded}(f,[a,b]).
  \]
\end{description}

The displayed obstruction is the corresponding failure mode.
  \[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } a<b \text{ and } f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}.\\
&\Bigl(\forall c\in[a,b]\;\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta>0\;\forall x\in[a,b]\bigl(|x-c|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon\bigr)\Bigr)\\
&\qquad\land \Bigl(\forall M>0\;\exists x\in[a,b]\;(|f(x)|>M)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
  \]
  \[
\operatorname{IsContinuous}(f,[a,b],\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) \land \neg\operatorname{Bounded}(f,[a,b]).
  \]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Continuity ties nearby inputs to nearby outputs, and the compact interval $[a,b]$ can be covered by finitely many neighborhoods in which the oscillation of $f$ is controlled; taking the maximal oscillation among this finite cover supplies a global bound. Failure typically arises when the domain lacks compactness: an omitted endpoint allows the function to escape control near the hole, an unbounded interval lets values diverge along the ray, and a point of discontinuity can spike the function without upsetting nearby behavior elsewhere.

nodes.name: Absolute Maximum and Absolute Minimum
nodes.statement_display: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $f \colon A \to \mathbb{R}$. A point $x^{*} \in A$ is an absolute maximum of $f$ on $A$ if and only if $f(x^{*}) \ge f(x)$ for every $x \in A$. A point $x_{*} \in A$ is an absolute minimum of $f$ on $A$ if and only if $f(x_{*}) \le f(x)$ for every $x \in A$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A \subseteq \mathbb{R},\; f \colon A \to \mathbb{R},\; x^{*}, x_{*} \in A.\\
&x^{*} \text{ is an absolute maximum of } f \text{ on } A
\Longleftrightarrow \forall x \in A\; (f(x) \le f(x^{*})).\\
&x_{*} \text{ is an absolute minimum of } f \text{ on } A
\Longleftrightarrow \forall x \in A\; (f(x_{*}) \le f(x)).
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
&(x^{*} \in A) \land \operatorname{GreatestElement}(f(x^{*}),f(A),\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq))
\Longleftrightarrow (x^{*} \in A) \land \forall x \in A\; (f(x) \le f(x^{*})),\\
&(x_{*} \in A) \land \operatorname{LeastElement}(f(x_{*}),f(A),\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq))
\Longleftrightarrow (x_{*} \in A) \land \forall x \in A\; (f(x_{*}) \le f(x)).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.body_tex: An absolute maximum identifies the highest value that $f$ attains on its domain $A$, together with a point of attainment, and the absolute minimum identifies the lowest attained value. These extrema describe the global ceiling and floor of the graph restricted to $A$, so they are the endpoints of the vertical range. Failure occurs either when the candidate point is not part of the domain or when another domain point produces a superior value, reflecting that global optimization is sensitive to both membership and comparative size. Geometrically the absolute maximum sits at the tallest point of the graph above $A$, while the absolute minimum sits at the lowest point.

nodes.name: Extreme Value Theorem
nodes.statement_display: Let $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous. There exist points $x_m,x_M \in [a,b]$ such that $f(x_m) \le f(x) \le f(x_M)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$. Equivalently, $f$ attains both an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on $[a,b]$.

\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
The theorem can fail if the compact interval hypothesis is lost, or if
the function is not continuous on the whole interval. Without compactness
an extremal value may exist only as a limiting value, and without
continuity the graph may jump over its supremum or infimum.


  \item[\(\operatorname{IsContinuous}.\)]
  The formal obstruction is failure of the continuity hypothesis used by the conclusion.
  \[
  \exists c\in A\;\exists\varepsilon_0>0\;\forall\delta>0\;\exists x\in A\;
  \bigl(|x-c|<\delta\land |f(x)-f(c)|\ge\varepsilon_0\bigr).
  \]
  \[
  \neg\,\operatorname{IsContinuous}(f,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}).
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Continuity on a closed and bounded interval forces the image of the interval to inherit the compact features of the domain. The function cannot escape to infinity or oscillate without settling, so it must reach both its highest and lowest values somewhere in the interval. When the hypotheses fail, the typical obstruction is the loss of compactness: on an open interval the function might drift off without achieving its supremum, and without continuity it may jump over candidate extrema.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Continuity forces the image of the interval $[a,b]$ to contain every intermediate value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$. A sign change therefore compels the graph to cross the horizontal axis, producing a root strictly inside the interval. Failure occurs when the endpoint values share the same sign or when $f$ is not continuous, because then the image need not sweep across zero. Geometrically, the theorem asserts that a continuous curve connecting opposite sides of the $x$-axis must intersect the axis somewhere in between.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: A continuous real-valued function on an interval cannot skip any intermediate scalar between two attained values, so the graph must cross every horizontal level that lies strictly between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$. The conclusion provides an interior point $c$ whose image equals the prescribed level $k$, ensuring root-finding for $f-k$. If the hypothesis fails, either $f$ is not continuous or the level $k$ does not lie between the endpoint values, and no such interior point need exist.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall a,b\in\mathbb{R}\;\forall f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}:\\
&\qquad
\Bigl(a<b \land
\forall c\in[a,b]\;\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta>0\;\forall x\in[a,b]\;
\bigl(|x-c|<\delta\Rightarrow |f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon\bigr)\Bigr)
\Longrightarrow
f([a,b])=[\min_{[a,b]} f,\max_{[a,b]} f].
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The statement combines the extreme value theorem, which supplies both a minimum and a maximum on $[a,b]$, with the intermediate value theorem, which fills in every intermediate value between them. Consequently the image $f([a,b])$ is a closed interval with endpoints given by the absolute extremal values of $f$ on $[a,b]$, showing that continuous functions map compact intervals onto compact intervals without introducing gaps.

A continuous function on a compact interval cannot oscillate across a level c without actually attaining that level. Stated contrapositive fashion, if c is never taken then the entire graph lies strictly above or strictly below the horizontal line y=c. The only way this guarantee can fail is when the function produces values on both sides of c, in which case continuity forces a crossing point. Geometrically the conclusion describes the image of a connected set under a continuous map: it is an interval, so omitting c forces the image to stay in one of the open half-lines determined by c.

A continuous function on a compact interval cannot oscillate across a level c without actually attaining that level. Stated contrapositive fashion, if c is never taken then the entire graph lies strictly above or strictly below the horizontal line y=c. The only way this guarantee can fail is when the function produces values on both sides of c, in which case continuity forces a crossing point. Geometrically the conclusion describes the image of a connected set under a continuous map: it is an interval, so omitting c forces the image to stay in one of the open half-lines determined by c.

need lie within $\varepsilon$ of $L$. The input condition here is
$\operatorname{Within}$ --- unpunctured. The limit definition replaces
this with a punctured centered interval condition and asserts
that for every $\varepsilon$ such a $\delta$ exists.

nodes.name: Limit of a Function
nodes.statement_display:
Let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c$ be a cluster point of $A$.
A real number $L$ is the \textbf{limit of $f$ at $c$}, written
$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$, if
\[
  \forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists\delta>0\;\forall x\in A\;
  0<|x-c|<\delta\Rightarrow |f(x)-L|<\varepsilon.
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
Define
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \varepsilon>0
  &\Longleftrightarrow \varepsilon\text{ is an output tolerance},\\
  \delta>0
  &\Longleftrightarrow \delta\text{ is an input tolerance},\\
  \operatorname{IsPuncturedCenteredOpenInterval}
  (I^\times_\delta(c),I_\delta(c),c,\delta,\mathbb R)
  &\quad\text{and}\quad
  \operatorname{Within}(x,I^\times_\delta(c),\mathbb R)
  &\Longleftrightarrow 0<|x-c|<\delta,\\
  \operatorname{IsCenteredOpenInterval}
  (I_\varepsilon(L),L,\varepsilon,\mathbb R)
  &\quad\text{and}\quad
  \operatorname{Within}(y,I_\varepsilon(L),\mathbb R)
  &\Longleftrightarrow |y-L|<\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{TendsTo}(f,A,c,L,\mathbb{R})
  &\Longleftrightarrow
  \forall \varepsilon\,
  \Bigl(
    \varepsilon>0
    \Rightarrow
    \exists \delta\,
    \bigl(
      \delta>0
      \wedge
      \forall x\in A\,
      [
        \operatorname{Within}(x,I^\times_\delta(c),\mathbb R)
        \Rightarrow
        \operatorname{Within}(f(x),I_\varepsilon(L),\mathbb R)
      ]
    \bigr)
  \Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

    \bigr)

    0<|x-c|<\delta
    \wedge
    |f(x)-L|\geq\varepsilon_0

\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The quantifier structure is asymmetric by design. The output
tolerance $\varepsilon$ is a \emph{demand}: the caller specifies how
precise the output must be. The input tolerance $\delta$ is a
\emph{response}: the definition asserts one always exists. The input
condition is punctured because $f$ may not be defined at $c$, and
because continuity --- not limits --- is the concept that includes $c$
itself. This is the deepest structural difference between the two
definitions. Four critical features: (i) $f$ need not be defined at
$c$; (ii) $c$ must be a cluster point of $A$ else the condition is
vacuously satisfied by every $L$; (iii) $\delta$ may depend on
$\varepsilon$; (iv) the condition is about all $x$ near $c$
simultaneously, not just one.

nodes.name: Sequential Definition of Limit
nodes.statement_display:
Let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c$ be a cluster point of $A$.
The limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ in the \textbf{sequential
sense} holds if for every sequence $(x_n) \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$
with $x_n \to c$, the sequence $(f(x_n))$ converges to $L$.

nodes.name: Centered Interval Form of Limit
nodes.statement_display:
Let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c$ be a cluster point of $A$.
The limit $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=L$ in the \textbf{centered interval
sense} holds if for every centered open interval
$I_\varepsilon(L)$ there exists a punctured centered open interval
$I_\delta^\times(c)$ such that
\[
  x\in I_\delta^\times(c)\cap A
  \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
  f(x)\in I_\varepsilon(L).
\]

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
Failure of uniqueness would mean that two distinct real numbers both satisfy
the limit definition at the same cluster point.


  \item[\(\operatorname{TendsTo}.\)]
  The formal obstruction is failure of the limit predicate at the stated point.
  \[
  \exists\varepsilon_0>0\;\forall\delta>0\;\exists x\in A\;
  \bigl(0<|x-c|<\delta\land |f(x)-L|\ge\varepsilon_0\bigr).
  \]

  \neg\,\operatorname{TendsTo}(f,c,L,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}).
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
Non-uniqueness would require two values $L \neq L'$ each satisfying
the limit definition. The $\varepsilon = |L-L'|/2$ argument shows
any $x$ within $\min(\delta_1,\delta_2)$ of $c$ satisfies both
$|f(x)-L| < \varepsilon$ and $|f(x)-L'| < \varepsilon$, but then
$|L-L'| \leq |L-f(x)|+|f(x)-L'| < 2\varepsilon = |L-L'|$, a
contradiction. The cluster point condition is essential: it guarantees
such an $x$ exists.


  \item[\(\operatorname{TendsTo}.\)]
  The displayed obstruction is the predicate-level failure condition.
  \[
  \exists\varepsilon_0>0\;\forall\delta>0\;\exists x\in A\;
  \bigl(0<|x-c|<\delta\land |f(x)-L|\ge\varepsilon_0\bigr).
  \]

  \]
\end{description}

behavior of $f$ near $c$. Uniqueness is what licenses writing

$(x_n)\subseteq A\setminus\{c\}$ with $x_n\to c$, one has
$f(x_n)\to L$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The Sequential Criterion is the engine of the algebra of limits.
Once it is in hand:
\[
  \text{algebra of sequence limits}
  \;\xRightarrow{\text{Sequential Criterion}}\;
  \text{algebra of function limits.}
\]
Every sequence result --- sum, product, quotient, squeeze --- transfers
to function limits by feeding a sequence into the criterion and
reading the result back. The negation is equally powerful: to
disprove $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=L$, exhibit one sequence
$(x_n) \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$ with $x_n \to c$ and
$f(x_n) \not\to L$.

nodes.name: Limit Implies Local Boundedness
nodes.statement_display:
Let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c$ be a cluster point of $A$.
If $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=L$ for some $L \in \mathbb{R}$,
then there exist $\delta, M > 0$ such that $|f(x)| \leq M$ for all
$x \in A$ with $0<|x-c|<\delta$.

Let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c$ be a cluster point of $A$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
If every nearby value of $f$ is trapped in $[a,b]$, the limit cannot
escape outside $[a,b]$. This is the function-limit analogue of the
sequence result that limits preserve non-strict inequalities. The
proof applies the Sequential Criterion and that sequence result
directly.

$A$. Suppose $\lim_{x\to c}f(x)=L =

$\delta_0 > 0$ such that
\[

  f(x) \leq h(x) \leq g(x).
\]
Then $\lim_{x\to c}h(x)=L$.

nodes.statement_display:

point of $E$, let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $\delta > 0$.
Then
\[
  \lim_{x\to x_0;\,x\in E}f(x)=L
  \;\iff\;
  \lim_{x\to x_0;\,x\in E\cap(x_0-\delta,x_0+\delta)}f(x)=L.
\]

nodes.name: Monotone Limit Theorem
nodes.statement_display:
Let $a < b$ and let $f : (a,b) \to \mathbb{R}$ be monotone and
bounded. Then both one-sided limits exist at every interior point.
For increasing $f$ and every $x_0 \in (a,b)$:
\[
  f(x_0^-) = \sup\{\,f(x) : a < x < x_0\,\},
  \qquad
  f(x_0^+) = \inf\{\,f(x) : x_0 < x < b\,\}.
\]

Predicate reading
Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Boundedness guarantees the supremum and infimum used as candidate
limits exist. Monotonicity forces convergence toward them from each
side: for increasing $f$, the values $f(x)$ for $x < x_0$ form a
bounded increasing net approaching their supremum. No oscillation is
possible. The theorem establishes that monotone functions can only
have jump discontinuities --- never oscillatory ones.

Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The Cauchy criterion tests limit existence without knowing $L$. Two
outputs from any sufficiently small punctured ball must lie within
$\varepsilon$ of each other --- the outputs cluster even if their
common limit is unknown. This is the function-limit analogue of the
Cauchy completeness criterion for sequences, and relies on the
completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ in exactly the same way.

\]

nodes.name: Infinite Adherent Points
nodes.statement_display:

and only if for every $M\in\mathbb{R}$ there exists $x\in X$ such that
$x>M$. The point $-\infty$ is adherent to $X$ if and only if for every
$M\in\mathbb{R}$ there exists $x\in X$ such that $x<M$.

nodes.name: Limit at Infinity
nodes.statement_display:
Let $X \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be such that for every $M \in \mathbb{R}$ there exists $x \in X$ with $x > M$, let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. The limit of $f$ at $+\infty$ equals $L$ if and only if
for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $M \in \mathbb{R}$ such that for every $x \in X$, $x > M$ implies $|f(x) - L| < \varepsilon$.

nodes.name: Limits Superior and Inferior of a Function
nodes.statement_display:
Let $f:E\to\mathbb{R}$ and let $x_0$ be an accumulation point of $E$. For each $\delta>0$ set
\[
U(\delta)=\{\,f(x): x\in E,\ 0<|x-x_0|<\delta\,\}.
\]
The extended real numbers $\limsup_{x\to x_0} f(x)$ and $\liminf_{x\to x_0} f(x)$ are defined by
\[
\limsup_{x\to x_0} f(x)=\inf_{\delta>0}\sup U(\delta),
\qquad
\liminf_{x\to x_0} f(x)=\sup_{\delta>0}\inf U(\delta),
\]
where each inner supremum or infimum is taken in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ and the outer infimum or supremum ranges over all $\delta>0$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The limit superior records the smallest height that eventually dominates all nearby function values, while the limit inferior records the largest depth that eventually underestimates all nearby values. Taking suprema within punctured neighborhoods captures every oscillation that can be witnessed arbitrarily close to $x_0$, and the outer infimum or supremum squeezes these oscillations to the sharpest possible bounds. Failure occurs only if the neighborhood sampling breaks down or if the oscillations race off to infinite extremal heights, signaling that no finite envelope can control the function near the accumulation point.

\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\;\forall f:A\to\mathbb{R}\;\forall x_0\in\mathbb{R}:\\
&\qquad
\Bigl(\forall \eta>0\;\exists x\in A\setminus\{x_0\}\;(|x-x_0|<\eta)\Bigr)
\Longrightarrow
\limsup_{x\to x_0} f(x) \ge \liminf_{x\to x_0} f(x).
\end{aligned}
\]

\Longrightarrow
\limsup_{x\to x_0} f(x) \ge \liminf_{x\to x_0} f(x).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The limsup records the largest cluster value that $f$ attains near $x_0$, while the liminf records the smallest cluster value. Because every subsequential limit contributing to the liminf also contributes to the limsup, the supremum of all cluster values cannot lie below their infimum. The only way equality holds is when all cluster values coincide, i.e. when the ordinary limit exists.

nodes.name: Limit Exists iff $\limsup=\liminf$
nodes.statement_display: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f \colon A \to \mathbb{R}$, let $x_0$ be a limit point of $A$ with $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$. support_blocks.body_tex: The two-sided limit of a real-valued function at a finite limit point exists precisely when the largest subsequential accumulation value and the smallest subsequential accumulation value coincide, in which case they both equal the limit. If the limsup exceeds the liminf, as happens for $f(x) = \sin(1/x)$ near $x_0 = 0$, the function oscillates between distinct cluster heights and therefore has no finite limit. The theorem isolates the limit as the unique height compatible with every oscillatory envelope and shows that agreeing envelopes are the exact signature of convergence in this local setting.

nodes.name: One-Sided Limits of Monotone Functions
nodes.statement_display:
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $c$ be interior to $I$, and let $f:I\to\mathbb{R}$ be increasing. Define
\[
L_- \coloneqq \sup\{f(x): x\in I,\; x<c\},
\qquad
L_+ \coloneqq \inf\{f(x): x\in I,\; c<x\}.
\]
Then both one-sided limits exist and satisfy
\[
\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) = L_-,
\qquad
\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) = L_+.
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\land
\bigl(\forall x,y\in I\;\forall z\in\mathbb{R}\;(x<z<y\Rightarrow z\in I)\bigr)
\land f:I\to\mathbb{R}\\
&\land\bigl(\forall x,y\in I\;(x<y\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y))\bigr)
\land c\in I
\land \exists a,b\in I\;(a<c<b)\\
&\land L_- = \sup\{f(x): x\in I,\; x<c\}
\land L_+ = \inf\{f(x): x\in I,\; c<x\}\\
&\Longrightarrow\\
&\forall \varepsilon>0\; \exists \delta_- > 0\; \forall x\in I\; \bigl((0<c-x<\delta_- \land x<c) \Rightarrow |f(x)-L_-|<\varepsilon \bigr)\\
&\land \forall \varepsilon>0\; \exists \delta_+ > 0\; \forall x\in I\; \bigl((0<x-c<\delta_+ \land c<x) \Rightarrow |f(x)-L_+|<\varepsilon \bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

&\text{Let } I\subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ be an interval, } f:I\to\mathbb{R} \text{ increasing, and } c \text{ interior to } I.\\
&\operatorname{LeftLimit}\!\Bigl(f,c,\sup\{f(x): x\in I,\; x<c\}\Bigr)
\land
\operatorname{RightLimit}\!\Bigl(f,c,\inf\{f(x): x\in I,\; x>c\}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: For an increasing function, the values just to the left of $c$ form a monotone increasing set bounded above by any right neighborhood, so their supremum matches the left-hand limit. Symmetrically, the values just to the right form a monotone increasing tail bounded below, making the infimum coincide with the right-hand limit. The theorem shows that monotonicity alone guarantees both one-sided limits exist and equals these extremal values. Failure occurs when $c$ is not an interior point or $f$ is not monotone, because the comparison sets may be empty or oscillatory, preventing the suprema or infima from governing the boundary behavior.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: A monotone graph possesses finite one-sided limits at every interior point. Continuity at $c$ demands that these approach values exactly meet the function value, so the graph neither overshoots nor undershoots when passing through $c$. Any failure manifests as a jump discontinuity: the graph either leaps upward at $c$ or remains below the right-hand approach. This criterion is indispensable when classifying discontinuities of monotone functions, since it converts continuity into a simple equality check between the function value and the adjacent plateau levels.

nodes.name: Jump of a Function
nodes.statement_display:
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $f:I\to\mathbb{R}$ be
increasing, and let $c$ be an interior point of $I$. If the one-sided
limits $f(c^-)$ and $f(c^+)$ exist, the jump of $f$ at $c$ is
\[
j_f(c)\coloneqq f(c^+)-f(c^-).
\]

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\;\forall f:I\to\mathbb{R}\;\forall c\in I\;\forall j\in\mathbb{R}\\
&\Bigl[
\bigl(\forall x,y\in I\;\forall z\in\mathbb{R}\;(x<z<y\Rightarrow z\in I)\bigr)
\land \exists a,b\in I\;(a<c<b)\\
&\qquad\land \bigl(\forall x,y\in I\;(x<y\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y))\bigr)
\land \exists L_-,L_+\in\mathbb{R}\;
\bigl(\lim_{x\to c^-}f(x)=L_- \land \lim_{x\to c^+}f(x)=L_+\bigr)
\Bigr]\\
&\qquad\Rightarrow
\bigl(j=j_f(c)\Longleftrightarrow j=f(c^+)-f(c^-)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  f\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  c\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\\
\operatorname{IsInterval}(I,\mathbb{R})
\land \operatorname{OrderPreserving}(f,I,\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq))
\land \operatorname{IsInterior}(c,I,\mathbb{R})
\land \exists L_-,L_+\in\mathbb{R}\;
\bigl(\operatorname{LeftLimit}(f,c,L_-,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})
\land \operatorname{RightLimit}(f,c,L_+,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})
\land j=L_+-L_-\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\;\forall f:I\to\mathbb{R}\;\forall c\in I\;\forall j\in\mathbb{R}:\\
&\neg\bigl(j=j_f(c)\bigr)
\Longleftrightarrow
\neg\bigl(\forall x,y\in I\;\forall z\in\mathbb{R}\;(x<z<y\Rightarrow z\in I)\bigr)\\
&\qquad\lor
\neg\bigl(\forall x,y\in I\;(x<y\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y))\bigr)
\lor \neg\bigl(\exists a,b\in I\;(a<c<b)\bigr)\\
&\qquad\lor
\forall L_-,L_+\in\mathbb{R}\;
\bigl(\lim_{x\to c^-}f(x)\ne L_-
\lor \lim_{x\to c^+}f(x)\ne L_+
\lor j\ne L_+-L_-\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

The displayed obstruction is the corresponding failure mode.
  \[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\;\forall f:I\to\mathbb{R}\;\forall c\in I\;\forall j\in\mathbb{R}:\\
&\neg\bigl(j=j_f(c)\bigr)
\Longleftrightarrow
\neg\bigl(\forall x,y\in I\;\forall z\in\mathbb{R}\;(x<z<y\Rightarrow z\in I)\bigr)\\
&\qquad\lor
\neg\bigl(\forall x,y\in I\;(x<y\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y))\bigr)
\lor \neg\bigl(\exists a,b\in I\;(a<c<b)\bigr)\\
&\qquad\lor
\forall L_-,L_+\in\mathbb{R}\;
\bigl(\lim_{x\to c^-}f(x)\ne L_-
\lor \lim_{x\to c^+}f(x)\ne L_+
\lor j\ne L_+-L_-\bigr).
\end{aligned}
  \]
  \[
\neg\operatorname{IsInterval}(I,\mathbb{R})
\lor \neg\operatorname{OrderPreserving}(f,I,\mathsf{OrderedSet}(\mathbb{R},\leq))
\lor \neg\operatorname{IsInterior}(c,I,\mathbb{R})
\lor
\forall L_-,L_+\in\mathbb{R}\;
\bigl(\neg\operatorname{LeftLimit}(f,c,L_-,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})
\lor \neg\operatorname{RightLimit}(f,c,L_+,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})
\lor j\ne L_+-L_-\bigr).
  \]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
For a monotone function the one-sided limits exist at every interior
point, and their difference measures the vertical gap in the graph at
that point. A zero jump means the two limiting heights agree; a positive
jump records a discontinuity of first kind.

logical_blocks.standard_quantified_statement:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\;\forall f:I\to\mathbb{R}\;\forall c\in I\;\forall j\in\mathbb{R}\\
&\Bigl[
\bigl(\forall x,y\in I\;\forall z\in\mathbb{R}\;(x<z<y\Rightarrow z\in I)\bigr)
\land \exists a,b\in I\;(a<c<b)\\
&\qquad\land \bigl(\forall x,y\in I\;(x<y\Rightarrow f(x)\le f(y))\bigr)
\land \exists L_-,L_+\in\mathbb{R}\;
\bigl(\lim_{x\to c^-}f(x)=L_- \land \lim_{x\to c^+}f(x)=L_+\bigr)
\Bigr]\\
&\qquad\Rightarrow
\bigl(j=j_f(c)\Longleftrightarrow j=f(c^+)-f(c^-)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.name: Discontinuities of a Monotone Function Are of First Kind
nodes.statement_display: Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $f:I \to \mathbb{R}$ be monotone, and let $a \in I$ be such that there exist points of $I$ strictly less and strictly greater than $a$. If $f$ is discontinuous at $a$, then both one-sided limits $\lim_{x\uparrow a} f(x)$ and $\lim_{x\downarrow a} f(x)$ exist in $\mathbb{R}$.

Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  f\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  a\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  I\subseteq\mathbb{R},\\
\operatorname{Monotone}\bigl(f,\mathsf{OrderedSet}(I,\leq)\bigr) \land \operatorname{IsDiscontinuous}(f,a,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) \Longrightarrow \exists L^{-},L^{+} \in \mathbb{R} \; \bigl(\operatorname{LeftLimit}(f,a,L^{-},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) \land \operatorname{RightLimit}(f,a,L^{+},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: A monotone graph can jump only by settling on distinct finite one-sided limits; it cannot oscillate wildly or blow up to infinity at a point of discontinuity. Thus every discontinuity of a monotone function is a jump discontinuity of the first kind, which explains why such functions are easy to integrate and why their exceptional sets are well behaved. Geometrically, the graph approaches a finite height from the left and another finite height from the right before making the jump.

nodes.name: Jump Intervals Are Disjoint
nodes.statement_display: Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval and let $f:I \to \mathbb{R}$ be nondecreasing. If $a,b \in I$ are distinct points of discontinuity of $f$, then the open intervals $(f(a^-),f(a^+))$ and $(f(b^-),f(b^+))$ are disjoint.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Every discontinuity of a monotone function is a jump discontinuity with a nondegenerate vertical gap $(f(c^-),f(c^+))$. Distinct discontinuities yield pairwise disjoint gaps, and each such interval contains a rational number. Associating to every discontinuity the rational number inside its gap produces an injection of the discontinuity set into $\mathbb{Q}$, forcing the set to be countable. The only way the conclusion could fail would be the existence of uncountably many disjoint jump intervals, which is impossible because the rationals are countable.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: A monotone function on a closed interval can only jump at most countably many times, so the points of discontinuity leave room inside every subinterval for a continuity point. Thus, although the function may fail to be continuous at isolated or countably many locations, continuity still occurs throughout any interval one inspects. This property ensures that monotone functions retain many features of continuous functions when arguments depend only on dense sets of continuity points.

nodes.name: Continuous Injective Is Strictly Monotone
nodes.statement_display: Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$. Then $f$ is injective if and only if $f$ is strictly monotone on $[a,b]$.

support_blocks.title: Standard quantified statement
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } f:[a,b]\to\mathbb{R} \text{ be continuous on } [a,b].\\
&\bigl[\forall x,y\in[a,b]\;(f(x)=f(y)\Rightarrow x=y)\bigr] \Longleftrightarrow
\bigl[\forall x,y\in[a,b]\;(x<y\Rightarrow f(x)<f(y))\bigr]\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\lor
\bigl[\forall x,y\in[a,b]\,(x<y\Rightarrow f(y)<f(x))\bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  f\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\\
\operatorname{IsContinuous}(f,[a,b],\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) \Longrightarrow
\bigl(\operatorname{Injective}(f,A,\mathbb{R}) \Longleftrightarrow
\operatorname{StrictlyMonotone}(f,[a,b])\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: A continuous function on a closed interval cannot reverse direction without repeating a value, so injectivity enforces a single increasing or decreasing trend across the entire domain. Conversely any strictly monotone map is automatically injective. The result emphasizes that topological constraints supplied by continuity interact with order-theoretic injectivity to force global monotonicity; failure occurs precisely when the graph turns back on itself, producing repeated values. Geometrically the continuous injective graph must cross each horizontal line at most once, which is only possible when the graph rises everywhere or falls everywhere.

&\text{Let } I\subseteq\mathbb{R} \text{ be an interval and } f:I\to\mathbb{R}.\\
&\Bigl[(\forall x,y\in I)(x<y \Rightarrow f(x)<f(y)) \land \forall c\in I\;\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta>0\;\forall x\in I\bigl(|x-c|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon\bigr)\Bigr]\\
&\quad\Longrightarrow \Bigl[\exists g:f(I)\to I \text{ such that } (\forall x\in I)\, g(f(x))=x \land (\forall y\in f(I))\, f(g(y))=y\\
&\qquad\land (\forall u,v\in f(I))(u<v \Rightarrow g(u)<g(v)) \land \forall y\in f(I)\;\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \eta>0\;\forall u\in f(I)\bigl(|u-y|<\eta \Rightarrow |g(u)-g(y)|<\varepsilon\bigr)\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: A continuous strictly monotone function on an interval never reverses the order of points, so it is automatically bijective onto its image. This theorem records that the inverse map retains the same order orientation and inherits continuity, reflecting the fact that no sudden jumps can occur when the original graph crosses each horizontal line exactly once. Failure would require either loss of monotonicity or a discontinuity, either of which would create a flat spot or a jump preventing the existence of a continuous inverse. Geometrically, the graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ across the diagonal line $y=x$, so the smoothness and strict increase or decrease are visibly preserved by symmetry.

nodes.name: Relative Neighborhood
nodes.statement_display: Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $a \in E$. A set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a neighborhood of $a$ in $E$ if and only if there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $U = E \cap (a-\delta, a+\delta)$. Equivalently, every neighborhood of $a$ in $E$ is a set of the form $U_E(a) := E \cap (a-\delta, a+\delta)$ for some $\delta > 0$.

nodes.name: Continuity at a Point
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $c \in A$. The function $f$ is \textbf{continuous at $c$} if and only if
\[
\forall \varepsilon > 0 \;\exists \delta > 0 \;\forall x \in A :
\bigl(|x-c| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-f(c)| < \varepsilon\bigr).
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
Continuity at $c$ fails precisely when there exists a persistent output gap $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that no matter how small the chosen centered interval about $c$ is, a point of $A$ within that interval keeps the function values at least $\varepsilon_0$ away from $f(c)$. The single failure branch records this inescapable oscillation near $c$.

\bigl(|x-c|<\delta \land |f(x)-f(c)| \ge \varepsilon_0\bigr).

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Continuity at $c$ means that the output $f(x)$ can be kept arbitrarily close to $f(c)$ by taking $x$ sufficiently close to $c$ while staying in the domain $A$. The negated form highlights that a discontinuity arises only when there is a fixed positive separation in output that persists no matter how tightly one zooms in on $c$, so nearby inputs cannot force the outputs to settle near $f(c)$. This captures the geometric intuition that the graph of a continuous function has no abrupt jumps or breaks at $c$.

The negation says that one tolerance band resists every centered-interval choice, so some sequence of points from $A$ approaches $c$ while their images either spike above or dip below $f(c)$ by at least a fixed amount. Geometrically, arbitrarily tight vertical strips around the graph above $c$ must be achievable by shrinking the horizontal window; failure means the graph keeps escaping that strip no matter how closely the input variable hugs $c$.

support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
Continuity at $c$ fails sequentially when there exists a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in $A$ with $x_n \to c$ but $f(x_n)$ does not converge to $f(c)$. This manifests in two distinct ways: either $f(x_n)$ converges to some limit different from $f(c)$, or $f(x_n)$ fails to converge entirely (oscillating without settling or diverging to infinity).


  \item[\(\operatorname{IsContinuous}.\)]
  The displayed obstruction is the corresponding failure mode.
  \[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A \subseteq \mathbb{R},\; c \in A,\; f \colon A \to \mathbb{R}.\\
&f \text{ is not continuous at } c \Longleftrightarrow
\exists (x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}} \subseteq A\;
\Bigl(\lim_{n\to\infty} x_n = c \land \lim_{n\to\infty} f(x_n) \ne f(c)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
  \]
  \[
\neg\operatorname{IsContinuous}(f,\mathsf{Point}(c,A),\mathbb R,\mathbb R)
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists x_n\;
\Bigl(\mathsf{Sequence}(x_n, A)
\land \operatorname{ConvergesTo}(x_n,c,\mathbb R)
\land \neg\operatorname{ConvergesTo}(f(x_n),f(c),\mathbb R)\Bigr).
  \]
\end{description}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The sequential characterization asserts that information about $f$ near $c$ is completely encoded by its action on limits of sequences taken within the domain. Any approach to $c$ through admissible points must transport convergent input sequences to convergent output sequences with the expected limit; conversely, a single pathological sequence suffices to expose a discontinuity. Geometrically, this captures the idea that $f$ cannot introduce jumps or oscillations that persist along every infinitesimal path toward $c$.

nodes.name: Neighbourhood Characterization of Discontinuity
nodes.statement_display: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f \colon A \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $c \in A$. The function $f$ is discontinuous at $c$ if and only if there exists a neighborhood $V$ of $f(c)$ such that for every neighborhood $U$ of $c$ relative to $A$ there exists $x \in U \cap A$ with $f(x) \notin V$.

nodes.name: Types of Discontinuity
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f:A \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $x_0 \in A$ with $f$ discontinuous at $x_0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
  \item \emph{Removable} iff $\exists L \in \mathbb{R}:\;\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = L$ and $L \ne f(x_0)$.
  \item \emph{Jump} iff $\exists L_{-}, L_{+} \in \mathbb{R}:\;\lim_{x \to x_0^-} f(x) = L_{-}$, $\lim_{x \to x_0^+} f(x) = L_{+}$, and $L_{-} \ne L_{+}$.
  \item \emph{Essential} iff it is not removable.
\end{enumerate}

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Removable } \Longleftrightarrow \exists L \in \mathbb{R}\; \bigl(\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = L \land L \ne f(x_0)\bigr).\\
&\text{Jump } \Longleftrightarrow \exists L_{-}, L_{+} \in \mathbb{R}\; \bigl(\lim_{x \to x_0^-} f(x) = L_{-} \land \lim_{x \to x_0^+} f(x) = L_{+} \land L_{-} \ne L_{+}\bigr).\\
&\text{Essential } \Longleftrightarrow \neg \exists L \in \mathbb{R}\; \bigl(\lim_{x \to x_0} f(x) = L \land L \ne f(x_0)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  f\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  A\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\\
\operatorname{IsRemovableDiscontinuity}(f,x_0,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) &\coloneqq \exists L \in \mathbb{R}\; \bigl(\operatorname{TendsTo}(f,A,x_0,L,\mathbb{R}) \land L \ne f(x_0)\bigr).\\
\operatorname{IsJumpDiscontinuity}(f,x_0,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) &\coloneqq \exists L_{-}, L_{+} \in \mathbb{R}\; \bigl(\operatorname{LeftLimit}(f,A,x_0,L_{-},\mathbb{R}) \land \operatorname{RightLimit}(f,A,x_0,L_{+},\mathbb{R}) \land L_{-} \ne L_{+}\bigr).\\
\operatorname{IsEssentialDiscontinuity}(f,x_0,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) &\coloneqq \neg \operatorname{IsRemovableDiscontinuity}(f,x_0,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}).
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.name: Oscillation on a Set
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, let $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$, and let
$E\subseteq A$. The oscillation of $f$ on $E$ is the extended real number
\[
\omega(f;E)\coloneqq
\sup\{\,|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|:x_1,x_2\in E\,\}
=\mathrm{diam}(f(E)).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
Oscillation on a set records the spread of the image --- the diameter
of $f(E)$. Small oscillation means all values of $f$ on $E$ lie
close together. Zero oscillation means $f$ is constant on $E$.

nodes.name: Oscillation at a Point
nodes.statement_display:
Let $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f:E \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $x_0 \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $U_\delta(x_0)\cap E \neq \varnothing$ for every $\delta>0$, where $U_\delta(x_0)=\{x \in \mathbb{R}: |x-x_0|<\delta\}$. The oscillation of $f$ at $x_0$ is the extended real number
\[
\omega(f;x_0)
=
\lim_{\delta \to 0^+}
\omega\bigl(f;\,U_\delta(x_0)\cap E\bigr),
\]
with $\omega(f;A)$ denoting the oscillation of $f$ on the set $A$. Because the function $\delta \mapsto \omega\bigl(f;\,U_\delta(x_0)\cap E\bigr)$ is nonincreasing, this right-hand limit exists (possibly $+\infty$).

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } E \subseteq \mathbb{R},\, f:E \to \mathbb{R},\, x_0 \in \mathbb{R},\, \omega \in [0,\infty].\\
&\bigl[(\forall \delta>0:\, U_\delta(x_0)\cap E \neq \varnothing)\ \land\ \omega(f;x_0)=\omega\bigr]\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
\forall \varepsilon>0\; \exists \delta>0\; \forall r\;(0<r<\delta \Rightarrow |\omega(f;U_r(x_0)\cap E)-\omega|<\varepsilon).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  f\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\\
\operatorname{Oscillation}(\omega,f,x_0,\mathbb{R}) \coloneqq
\lim_{\delta \to 0^+} \omega\bigl(f;\,U_\delta(x_0)\cap E\bigr) = \omega,
\quad U_\delta(x_0)=\{x \in \mathbb{R}: |x-x_0|<\delta\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

&\Longleftrightarrow
\Bigl[\exists \delta_0>0:\, U_{\delta_0}(x_0)\cap E = \varnothing\Bigr]\\

\end{aligned}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Oscillation at $x_0$ measures the largest possible jump in function values that survives after one zooms in arbitrarily tightly around $x_0$. The shrinking neighborhoods $U_r(x_0)\cap E$ supply finer and finer samples, and the oscillation on each such set records the spread of $f$ there. If these spreads settle to a single number, that number captures the local variability; it is zero precisely when $f$ becomes arbitrarily close to a single value, i.e., when $f$ is continuous at $x_0$. Failure occurs either because $x_0$ has no nearby domain points or because the spreads fluctuate indefinitely, reflecting wild local behavior.

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A \subseteq \mathbb{R},\; f \colon A \to \mathbb{R},\; c \in A.\\
&\left(\forall \varepsilon>0 \; \exists \delta>0 \; \forall x \in A \; \bigl(|x-c|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-f(c)|<\varepsilon\bigr)\right)\\
&\Longleftrightarrow\\
&\left(\inf_{\delta>0} \sup \bigl\{|f(x)-f(y)| : x,y \in A,\; |x-c|<\delta,\; |y-c|<\delta \bigr\} = 0\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The theorem states that measuring the oscillation of $f$ near $c$ captures exactly the same local regularity as the classical $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition of continuity. If oscillation collapses to zero, every pair of nearby function values becomes arbitrarily close, forcing $f(x)$ to approach $f(c)$. Conversely, any discontinuity manifests as a nonzero oscillation, because nearby points can produce separated outputs. The standard failure therefore arises from detecting a residual jump or oscillatory behavior in arbitrarily small neighborhoods of $c$.

nodes.name: Discontinuity Set via Oscillation
nodes.text_preview: Let $f:E\to\mathbb{R}$. Then \[ D(f):=\{x\in E: f \text{ is discontinuous at } x\} =\{x\in E: \omega(f;x)>0\} =\bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \{x\in E: \omega(f;x)\ge 1/n\}. \]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Oscillation detects discontinuity quantitatively: every discontinuity forces $\omega(f;x)$ to stay above some positive threshold, and conversely the vanishing of oscillation characterises continuity. Because each set $\{x\in E:\omega(f;x)\ge 1/n\}$ is closed, the discontinuity set $D(f)$ is an $F_{\sigma}$, a countable union of closed sets. This structural description is the gateway to measure-theoretic criteria such as the Lebesgue characterisation of Riemann integrability, where the size of $D(f)$ controls integrability.

nodes.name: Uniform Continuity
nodes.statement_display: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $f:A \to \mathbb{R}$. The function $f$ is uniformly continuous on $A$ if and only if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that for all $x,u \in A$ the implication $|x-u| < \delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-f(u)| < \varepsilon$ holds.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Uniform continuity demands that a single proximity scale $\delta$ answers any prescribed accuracy $\varepsilon$ simultaneously across the whole domain. The negation shows what goes wrong: a fixed output tolerance resists all choices of $\delta$ because pairs of nearby inputs can always be found that stretch the function values too far apart. Geometrically, the graph of a uniformly continuous function can be traversed with a ruler of length $\delta$ horizontally and $\varepsilon$ vertically without ever overstepping the vertical tolerance, whereas a nonuniformly continuous function exhibits spikes that defeat every fixed ruler length.

nodes.name: Algebra of Uniform Continuity on a General Domain
nodes.statement_display:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
  \item For every set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, every pair of functions $f,g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ that are uniformly continuous on $A$, and every scalar $c \in \mathbb{R}$, the functions $f+g$, $f-g$, and $cf$ are uniformly continuous on $A$.
  \item There exist a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and uniformly continuous functions $f,g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ such that the product $fg$ is not uniformly continuous on $A$.
\end{enumerate}

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\forall A \subseteq \mathbb{R}\; \forall f,g : A \to \mathbb{R}\; \forall c \in \mathbb{R}:\\
&\qquad
\Bigl[
\bigl(\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta_f>0\;\forall x,y\in A\;(|x-y|<\delta_f\Rightarrow |f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon)\bigr)\\
&\qquad\land
\bigl(\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta_g>0\;\forall x,y\in A\;(|x-y|<\delta_g\Rightarrow |g(x)-g(y)|<\varepsilon)\bigr)
\Bigr]
\Rightarrow
\Bigl[
\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta_1>0\;\forall x,y\in A\;(|x-y|<\delta_1\Rightarrow |(f+g)(x)-(f+g)(y)|<\varepsilon)\\
&\qquad\land
\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta_2>0\;\forall x,y\in A\;(|x-y|<\delta_2\Rightarrow |(f-g)(x)-(f-g)(y)|<\varepsilon)\\
&\qquad\land
\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta_3>0\;\forall x,y\in A\;(|x-y|<\delta_3\Rightarrow |cf(x)-cf(y)|<\varepsilon)
\Bigr],\\
&\exists A \subseteq \mathbb{R}\; \exists f,g : A \to \mathbb{R}:\;
\Bigl[
\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta_f>0\;\forall x,y\in A\;(|x-y|<\delta_f\Rightarrow |f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon)
\Bigr]\\
&\qquad\land
\Bigl[
\forall \varepsilon>0\;\exists \delta_g>0\;\forall x,y\in A\;(|x-y|<\delta_g\Rightarrow |g(x)-g(y)|<\varepsilon)
\Bigr]\\
&\qquad\land
\exists \varepsilon_0>0\;\forall \delta>0\;\exists x,y\in A\;
\bigl(|x-y|<\delta\land |f(x)g(x)-f(y)g(y)|\ge\varepsilon_0\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
  f\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  g\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  cf\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  fg\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\\
&\forall A \subseteq \mathbb{R}\; \forall f,g : A \to \mathbb{R}\; \forall c \in \mathbb{R}:\\
&\qquad\bigl(\operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(f,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R) \land \operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(g,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R)\bigr) \Longrightarrow \bigl(\operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(f+g,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R) \land \operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(f-g,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R) \land \operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(cf,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R)\bigr),\\
&\exists A \subseteq \mathbb{R}\; \exists f,g : A \to \mathbb{R}:\quad \operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(f,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R) \land \operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(g,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R) \land \neg \operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(fg,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R).
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Uniform continuity is stable under linear combinations on any common domain, so sums, differences, and scalar multiples inherit the same global control on oscillation from the original functions. The proof decomposes the linear expressions into epsilon-delta bounds that add and subtract without upsetting the uniform response. In contrast, products can amplify local variation when one factor lacks a bounded range, so even uniformly continuous multiplicands can produce a product that fails the global tolerance requirement. The theorem explains both the algebraic closure that analysts routinely exploit and the standard obstruction, guiding expectations when building uniformly continuous functions from simpler pieces.

nodes.name: Algebra of Uniform Continuity on a Bounded Domain
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be bounded, and let $f,g:A \to \mathbb{R}$ be uniformly continuous on $A$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The product $x \mapsto f(x)g(x)$ is uniformly continuous on $A$.
\item If there exists $k>0$ such that $|g(x)| \ge k$ for all $x \in A$, then the quotient $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$ is uniformly continuous on $A$.
\end{enumerate}

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ be bounded and } f,g:A \to \mathbb{R}.\\
&\bigl[\forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists \delta > 0\; \forall x,y \in A\;(|x-y|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon)\bigr]\\
&\land \bigl[\forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists \delta > 0\; \forall x,y \in A\;(|x-y|<\delta \Rightarrow |g(x)-g(y)|<\varepsilon)\bigr]\\
&\Rightarrow \forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists \delta > 0\; \forall x,y \in A\;(|x-y|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(x)g(x)-f(y)g(y)|<\varepsilon),\\
&\bigl[\forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists \delta > 0\; \forall x,y \in A\;(|x-y|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon)\bigr]\\
&\land \bigl[\forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists \delta > 0\; \forall x,y \in A\;(|x-y|<\delta \Rightarrow |g(x)-g(y)|<\varepsilon)\bigr]\\
&\land \bigl[\exists k>0\; \forall x \in A\;(|g(x)| \ge k)\bigr]\\
&\Rightarrow \forall \varepsilon > 0\; \exists \delta > 0\; \forall x,y \in A\;(|x-y|<\delta \Rightarrow |f(x)/g(x)-f(y)/g(y)|<\varepsilon).
\end{aligned}
\]

  f\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  g\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  fg\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\\
&\text{Assume } A \subseteq \mathbb{R} \text{ is bounded and } f,g:A \to \mathbb{R}.\\
&\operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(f,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R) \land \operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(g,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R)\\
&\qquad\Longrightarrow \operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(fg,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R),\\
&\operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(f,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R) \land \operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(g,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R) \land \exists k>0\;\forall x \in A\;(|g(x)| \ge k)\\
&\qquad\Longrightarrow \operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(f/g,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R).
\end{aligned}
\]

nodes.name: Sequential Characterization of Uniform Continuity
nodes.statement_display: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $f:A \to \mathbb{R}$. Then $f$ is uniformly continuous on $A$ if and only if for every pair of sequences $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ in $A$ with $\lim_{n \to \infty} (x_n - y_n) = 0$ we have $\lim_{n \to \infty} (f(x_n) - f(y_n)) = 0$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Uniform continuity prevents the function from pulling together inputs that are asymptotically identical while letting their images drift apart. The sequential formulation packages this requirement into a tail test that ignores explicit epsilon-delta bookkeeping: whenever two points of $A$ are eventually arbitrarily close, their function values must also be eventually arbitrarily close. Proving uniform continuity via sequences is often simpler, and conversely, producing two sequences that collide in $A$ but whose images do not collide gives a concrete witness that uniform continuity fails. The two failure modes correspond to breaking one direction or the other of the claimed equivalence.

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Uniform continuity controls the change in $f(x)$ solely through the distance between inputs, so any Cauchy sequence in the domain is sent to a sequence whose tails remain uniformly close. Ordinary pointwise continuity cannot guarantee this because the necessary input tolerance could shrink along the sequence, so uniformity is exactly the additional strength needed to transport the Cauchy property. The standard failure mode occurs when $f$ is merely continuous and the sequence approaches a boundary point where continuity loses uniform control, producing large oscillations in the image sequence. Geometrically, uniform continuity supplies a single modulus of continuity that works for the entire path traced by $(x_n)$, ensuring that eventually all image terms lie in an arbitrarily small common interval.

nodes.statement_display: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f:A \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $K>0$. The function $f$ satisfies the Lipschitz condition on $A$ with constant $K$ if and only if $|f(x)-f(u)| \le K|x-u|$ for every $x,u \in A$.

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The Lipschitz condition requires a single constant $K$ that simultaneously bounds the rate at which $f$ can stretch distances across the entire set $A$. It encapsulates a global slope cap: every secant line through the graph has absolute slope at most $K$. Failure occurs once a single pair of points forces a steeper secant, signaling that no uniform control constant works on the whole domain. Geometrically, the graph of a Lipschitz function lies inside a cone of opening determined by $K$, so nearby points cannot be blown apart faster than $K$ times their original spacing.

nodes.statement_display: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $f:A \to \mathbb{R}$. If there exists $K \ge 0$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)| \le K |x-y|$ for all $x,y \in A$, then $f$ is uniformly continuous on $A$.

Predicate reading
Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
If $f$ fails to be uniformly continuous on $A$, then $f$ is not Lipschitz on $A$ with any constant.
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A \subseteq \mathbb{R},\; f:A \to \mathbb{R}.\\
&\Bigl[\exists \varepsilon_0>0\;\forall \delta>0\;\exists x,y \in A\;(|x-y|<\delta \land |f(x)-f(y)|\ge\varepsilon_0)\Bigr]\\
&\Longrightarrow \forall K\ge 0\;\exists x,y \in A\;(|f(x)-f(y)|>K|x-y|).
\end{aligned}
\]


\[
\neg\operatorname{IsUniformlyContinuous}(f,A,\mathbb R,\mathbb R)
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\neg\exists K\ge 0:\;\operatorname{IsLipschitz}(f,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}).
\]


A Lipschitz bound controls the variation of $f$ by the distance between inputs with a single constant $K$, so the same $K$ yields a usable $\delta = \varepsilon/K$ for every pair of points at once, proving uniform continuity. When $K=0$ the function is constant and trivially uniform. Failure of uniform continuity would force two points arbitrarily close together whose images stay a fixed distance apart, contradicting the Lipschitz inequality.


The implication Lipschitz $\Rightarrow$ uniform continuity is strict. The canonical counterexample is $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ on $[0,1]$, which is uniformly continuous by the Heine--Cantor theorem but satisfies $|f(x)-f(0)|/|x-0| = 1/\sqrt{x} \to \infty$ as $x \to 0^+$, so no Lipschitz constant exists at the origin. This distinction is relevant to GPU Lipschitz-constant estimation: uniform continuity of a simulation function does not supply a computable $K$ for the Lipschitz condition; only an explicit Lipschitz bound does.

nodes.name: Algebra of Lipschitz Functions
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $f,g:A\to\mathbb{R}$ be Lipschitz with constants $K_f,K_g\ge 0$ respectively.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item For every $c\in\mathbb{R}$, the function $cf$ is Lipschitz on $A$ with constant $|c|K_f$.
\item The functions $f+g$ and $f-g$ are Lipschitz on $A$ with constant $K_f+K_g$.
\item If $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$, $h:B\to\mathbb{R}$ is Lipschitz with constant $K_h\ge 0$, and $f(A)\subseteq B$, then $h\circ f$ is Lipschitz on $A$ with constant $K_hK_f$.
\item If $|f(x)|\le M_f$ and $|g(x)|\le M_g$ for all $x\in A$, then $fg$ is Lipschitz on $A$ with constant $M_gK_f+M_fK_g$.
\item If $|f(x)|\le M_f$ for all $x\in A$, if $|g(x)|\ge k>0$ for all $x\in A$, and if $g$ is Lipschitz on $A$ with constant $K_g$, then $f/g$ is Lipschitz on $A$ with constant $K_f/k + M_fK_g/k^2$.
\end{enumerate}

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A\subseteq\mathbb{R},\; f,g:A\to\mathbb{R},\; K_f,K_g\ge 0,\\
&\forall x,y\in A:\ |f(x)-f(y)|\le K_f|x-y|\ \text{and}\ |g(x)-g(y)|\le K_g|x-y|.\\
&\text{(a) }\forall c\in\mathbb{R},\ \forall x,y\in A:\ |cf(x)-cf(y)|\le |c|K_f|x-y|.\\
&\text{(b) }\forall x,y\in A:\ |(f\pm g)(x)-(f\pm g)(y)|\le (K_f+K_g)|x-y|.\\
&\text{(c) }\text{If }B\subseteq\mathbb{R},\ f(A)\subseteq B,\ h:B\to\mathbb{R},\ \forall u,v\in B:\ |h(u)-h(v)|\le K_h|u-v|,\\
&\qquad\text{then }\forall x,y\in A:\ |h(f(x))-h(f(y))|\le K_hK_f|x-y|.\\
&\text{(d) }\text{If }|f(x)|\le M_f,\ |g(x)|\le M_g\ \forall x\in A,\ \text{then } \forall x,y\in A:\\
&\qquad |f(x)g(x)-f(y)g(y)|\le (M_gK_f+M_fK_g)|x-y|.\\
&\text{(e) }\text{If }|f(x)|\le M_f,\ |g(x)|\ge k>0\ \forall x\in A,\ \text{then }\forall x,y\in A:\\
&\qquad \left|\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}-\frac{f(y)}{g(y)}\right|\le \left(\frac{K_f}{k}+\frac{M_fK_g}{k^2}\right)|x-y|.
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Predicate reading
support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
  f\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  g\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  cf\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  h\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\qquad
  fg\colon A\to\mathbb{R},\\
&\operatorname{IsLipschitz}(f,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\land \operatorname{IsLipschitz}(g,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) \\
&\Longrightarrow \Bigl[\forall c\in\mathbb{R}:\operatorname{IsLipschitz}(cf,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\Bigr]\\
&\qquad\land \operatorname{IsLipschitz}(f+g,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\land \operatorname{IsLipschitz}(f-g,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\\
&\qquad\land \Bigl(\operatorname{IsLipschitz}(h,B,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\land f(A)\subseteq B\Rightarrow \operatorname{IsLipschitz}(h\circ f,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\Bigr)\\
&\qquad\land \Bigl[(|f|\le M_f)\land(|g|\le M_g)\Rightarrow \operatorname{IsLipschitz}(fg,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\Bigr]\\
&\qquad\land \Bigl[(|f|\le M_f)\land(|g|\ge k>0)\Rightarrow \operatorname{IsLipschitz}\!\left(\frac{f}{g},A,\frac{K_f}{k}+\frac{M_fK_g}{k^2}\right)\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: Lipschitz functions are stable under the standard algebraic operations: scaling magnifies the constant proportionally, addition and subtraction add the errors, and composition multiplies constants because distortions accumulate multiplicatively. Products and quotients require uniform control of magnitudes; bounds on the factors prevent growth in the coefficients that accompany the derivatives of the product rule heuristic, while a positive lower bound on the denominator guarantees the quotient does not amplify oscillations uncontrollably. Together, these clauses justify building rich classes of Lipschitz maps from simpler ones without losing quantitative control.

&\operatorname{IsLipschitz}(f,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\land \operatorname{IsLipschitz}(g,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}) \\
&\Longrightarrow \Bigl[\forall c\in\mathbb{R}:\operatorname{IsLipschitz}(cf,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\Bigr]\\
&\qquad\land \operatorname{IsLipschitz}(f+g,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\land \operatorname{IsLipschitz}(f-g,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\\
&\qquad\land \Bigl(\operatorname{IsLipschitz}(h,B,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\land f(A)\subseteq B\Rightarrow \operatorname{IsLipschitz}(h\circ f,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\Bigr)\\
&\qquad\land \Bigl[(|f|\le M_f)\land(|g|\le M_g)\Rightarrow \operatorname{IsLipschitz}(fg,A,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})\Bigr]\\
&\qquad\land \Bigl[(|f|\le M_f)\land(|g|\ge k>0)\Rightarrow \operatorname{IsLipschitz}\!\left(\frac{f}{g},A,\frac{K_f}{k}+\frac{M_fK_g}{k^2}\right)\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]
logical_blocks.interpretation: Lipschitz functions are stable under the standard algebraic operations: scaling magnifies the constant proportionally, addition and subtraction add the errors, and composition multiplies constants because distortions accumulate multiplicatively. Products and quotients require uniform control of magnitudes; bounds on the factors prevent growth in the coefficients that accompany the derivatives of the product rule heuristic, while a positive lower bound on the denominator guarantees the quotient does not amplify oscillations uncontrollably. Together, these clauses justify building rich classes of Lipschitz maps from simpler ones without losing quantitative control.

nodes.name: Bi-Lipschitz Map
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and let $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$. The map $f$ is bi-Lipschitz on $A$ if and only if there exist constants $0<\alpha\le K$ such that for every $x,u\in A$,
\[
\alpha|x-u|\le |f(x)-f(u)|\le K|x-u|.
\]
Any such pair $(\alpha,K)$ is called a bi-Lipschitz constant pair for $f$ on $A$.

nodes.name: Inverse of a Bi-Lipschitz Map Is Lipschitz
nodes.statement_display:
Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f:A \to \mathbb{R}$, and suppose there exist constants $\alpha,K>0$ such that
$\alpha |x-y| \le |f(x)-f(y)| \le K |x-y|$ for all $x,y \in A$. Then $f$ is injective, the inverse mapping $f^{-1}:f(A) \to A$ is well defined, and
\[
\frac{1}{K}|u-v| \le |f^{-1}(u)-f^{-1}(v)| \le \frac{1}{\alpha}|u-v|
\quad\text{for all } u,v \in f(A).
\]

support_blocks.body_tex:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\text{Let } A \subseteq \mathbb{R},\ f:A \to \mathbb{R},\ \alpha,K>0.\\
&\Bigl[\forall x,y \in A\;\bigl(\alpha |x-y| \le |f(x)-f(y)| \le K|x-y|\bigr)\Bigr]\\
&\Longrightarrow
\Bigl[\forall x,y \in A\;(f(x)=f(y) \Rightarrow x=y) \\
&\qquad\land \exists g:f(A)\to A\;\bigl(\forall u \in f(A)\;(f(g(u))=u)\bigr) \\
&\qquad\land \forall u,v \in f(A)\;\Bigl(\frac{1}{K}|u-v| \le |g(u)-g(v)| \le \frac{1}{\alpha}|u-v|\Bigr)\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: A bi-Lipschitz bound simultaneously controls the expansion and contraction of $f$, so no two points of $A$ can share the same image and the inverse is automatically a well-defined function on $f(A)$. The inequalities for $f^{-1}$ follow by applying the original bi-Lipschitz bounds to pairs of preimages, showing that reversing the mapping preserves the same type of two-sided Lipschitz control with the reciprocals of the original constants. Failure would require collapsing two distinct points or losing the two-sided bounds, either of which contradicts the defining hypothesis.

\[
(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c).
\]

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$. If $f$ and $g$ are differentiable at $c$, then $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$, and
\[
(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex: The Finite Linear Combination Rule is the full statement that differentiation is a \emph{linear operator}: it commutes with scalar multiplication and addition simultaneously, for any finite collection of differentiable functions. This is not a separate theorem from the Constant Multiple and Sum Rules --- it is their inductive closure. Stated in operator language: if $\mathcal{D}(I)$ denotes the vector space of functions differentiable at $c$, then $D_c : \mathcal{D}(I) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $D_c(f) = f'(c)$ is a linear functional. If every member of the finite family is differentiable on $I$, then their
finite linear combination differentiates term by term on $I$.
\[
\begin{aligned}

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The pointwise statements above --- each proved at a single point $c$ --- extend to global statements when the hypotheses hold at every point of $I$. If $f$ is differentiable on $I$, then $f' : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is itself a function and differentiation acts as a linear operator on the vector space $\mathcal{D}(I)$ of functions differentiable on $I$:
\[
  (\alpha f + \beta g)' = \alpha f' + \beta g',\qquad
  (fg)' = f'g + fg',\qquad
  \left(\frac{f}{g}\right)' = \frac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}.
\]
These equalities hold as functions on $I$. The Finite Linear Combination Rule in its global form is precisely the statement that $D : \mathcal{D}(I) \to \mathcal{F}(I)$ defined by $D(f) = f'$ is a linear map between function spaces, where $\mathcal{F}(I)$ denotes functions on $I$. The interval variants are not separate theorems --- they are the pointwise results collected into function notation by applying the pointwise result at each $x \in I$.

nodes.name: L'H\^{o}pital's Rule, \(0/0\) Form
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(a<b\), and let \(f,g:(a,b)\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable with \(g'(x)\neq 0\) for every \(x\in(a,b)\). Suppose
\[
  \lim_{x\to a^+}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^+}g(x)=0
  \qquad\text{and}\qquad
  \lim_{x\to a^+}\frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}=L
\]
for \(L\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\). Then
\[
  \lim_{x\to a^+}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)}=L.
\]
The analogous statements at left-hand endpoints, at two-sided interior points, and at infinity follow by the same reductions.

support_blocks.title: Failure modes
support_blocks.body_tex:
\begin{description}
  \item[Exposition.]
The rule is a one-way implication and is routinely misapplied.
\begin{itemize}
  \item \emph{Form not indeterminate.} If \(f/g\) is not genuinely \(0/0\),
        differentiating numerator and denominator can answer a different
        problem.
  \item \emph{\(\lim f'/g'\) fails to exist.} With \(f(x)=x+\sin x\) and
        \(g(x)=x\) as \(x\to+\infty\), the quotient \(f/g\to1\), but
        \(f'/g'=1+\cos x\) oscillates. Absence of \(\lim f'/g'\) says
        nothing by itself about \(\lim f/g\).
  \item \emph{\(g'\) vanishes near the target.} The denominator derivative
        must stay nonzero so the Cauchy Mean Value Theorem applies and the
        derivative ratio is defined.
\end{itemize}


  \item[\(\operatorname{Derivative}.\)]
  The displayed obstruction is the predicate-level failure condition.
  \[
  \exists\varepsilon_0>0\;\forall\delta>0\;\exists x\in A\;\bigl(0<|x-a|<\delta\land |Q_f(x)-D|\ge\varepsilon_0\bigr).
  \]
  \[
  \neg\,\operatorname{Derivative}(D,f,a,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R}).
  \]
\end{description}

nodes.name: Carath\'{e}odory Factorization
nodes.statement_display:
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $c \in I$. We say that $f$ admits a \emph{Carath\'{e}odory factorization} at $c$ if there exists a function $\phi : I \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, such that
\[
f(x) = f(c) + (x-c)\,\phi(x) \qquad \text{for all } x \in I.
\]
In this case, $f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $f'(c) = \phi(c)$.

Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The Carath\'{e}odory factorization replaces the difference quotient --- a function with a removable discontinuity at $c$ --- with a function $\phi$ that is genuinely continuous at $c$. The factorization $f(x)-f(c) = (x-c)\phi(x)$ holds everywhere on $I$, including at $x=c$ where both sides equal zero. The derivative is recovered as $\phi(c)$ without ever dividing by zero. This reframing converts analytical limit conditions into topological continuity conditions, which compose and factor more cleanly. It is the preferred tool for proving the product rule, quotient rule, and chain rule, because continuity of a product or composition is easier to establish than the existence of a limit of a quotient.

\medskip
\textbf{Carath\'{e}odory vs.\ Lipschitz.} Both control the increment $f(x)-f(c)$ by the factor $(x-c)$, but differently. The Carath\'{e}odory factorization requires the slope function $\phi(x)$ to extend \emph{continuously} to $c$; it controls the \emph{behaviour} of the slope, not just its size. The Lipschitz condition $|f(x)-f(c)| \leq L|x-c|$ only bounds the size of the increment. Carath\'{e}odory implies Lipschitz: if $\phi$ is continuous at $c$ it is bounded near $c$, so $|f(x)-f(c)| = |\phi(x)||x-c| \leq K|x-c|$ for some $K$ near $c$. The converse fails: $f(x)=|x|$ is Lipschitz on $\mathbb{R}$ with constant $1$ but the slope function takes values $\pm 1$ on either side of $0$ with no continuous extension.

nodes.name: Carath\'{e}odory Characterization of Differentiability
nodes.statement_display:
Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be an interval, let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$, and let $c \in I$. The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item $f$ is differentiable at $c$.
\item There exists a function $\phi : I \to \mathbb{R}$, continuous at $c$, such that
\[
f(x) = f(c) + (x-c)\,\phi(x) \qquad \text{for all } x \in I.
\]
\end{enumerate}
In this case, $\phi(c) = f'(c)$.

support_blocks.body_tex: This theorem establishes that differentiability and the existence of a Carath\'{e}odory factorization are exactly the same condition. The proof is a two-direction construction: in the forward direction, define $\phi$ as the difference quotient extended by $f'(c)$ at $c$ and verify continuity from the definition of the derivative; in the backward direction, recover the difference quotient from $\phi$ and read off its limit as $\phi(c)$. The theorem's power is that it converts every future differentiability argument into a continuity argument: to show $g \circ f$ is differentiable, find a continuous Carath\'{e}odory function for it; composing the Carath\'{e}odory functions of $f$ and $g$ yields one automatically.

\[
(g \circ f)'(c) = g'(f(c))\,f'(c).
\]

  \operatorname{IsDifferentiable}(f,c,\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})
  \land
  \operatorname{IsDifferentiable}(g,f(c),\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})
  \Longrightarrow
  (g\circ f)'(c)=g'(f(c))f'(c).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The derivative of a composition is the derivative of the outside function evaluated at the inside value, multiplied by the derivative of the inside function.


Let $\phi_f$ and $\phi_g$ be the Carath\'{e}odory slope factors for $f$ at $c$
and $g$ at $f(c)$. Then
\[
g(f(x))-g(f(c))
  =
\phi_g(f(x))(f(x)-f(c))
  =
\phi_g(f(x))\phi_f(x)(x-c).
\]
The new slope factor is
\[
  \phi_{g\circ f}(x)=\phi_g(f(x))\phi_f(x),
\]
which is continuous at $c$ and has value $g'(f(c))f'(c)$. This proof never
divides by $f(x)-f(c)$, so it avoids the failure in the informal
$\Delta g/\Delta f \cdot \Delta f/\Delta x$ argument when $f(x)=f(c)$ near
$c$.

nodes.statement_display:
Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an interval, let \(x\in I\), and suppose
that \(f,g:I\to\mathbb{R}\) are \(n\)-times differentiable on a
neighbourhood of \(x\). Then \(fg\) is \(n\)-times differentiable at \(x\),
and
\[
  (fg)^{(n)}(x)
  =
  \sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}f^{(k)}(x)g^{(n-k)}(x).
\]

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The binomial pattern is not an accident. Each of the \(n\) differentiations
lands on either \(f\) or \(g\), and \(\binom{n}{k}\) counts the ways to send
exactly \(k\) differentiations to \(f\). At \(n=1\), this is the ordinary
product rule.

nodes.name: Faa di Bruno's Formula
nodes.statement_display:
Let \(I,J\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be intervals, let \(x\in I\), suppose
\(g:I\to J\) is \(n\)-times differentiable on a neighbourhood of \(x\), and
suppose \(f:J\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(n\)-times differentiable on a neighbourhood
of \(g(x)\). Then \(f\circ g\) is \(n\)-times differentiable at \(x\), and
\[
  \frac{d^n}{dx^n}f(g(x))
  =
  \sum_{\sum_{m=1}^{n}mk_m=n}
  \frac{n!}{\prod_{m=1}^{n}k_m!\,(m!)^{k_m}}\,
  f^{(k)}(g(x))
  \prod_{m=1}^{n}\bigl(g^{(m)}(x)\bigr)^{k_m},
\]
where \(k_m\geq0\) and \(k=\sum_{m=1}^{n}k_m\).

support_blocks.title: Interpretation
support_blocks.body_tex:
The chain rule gives the first derivative of a composition. Repeated
differentiation is deeper: product-rule terms and chain-rule terms interlace,
and the bookkeeping is governed by integer partitions. Faa di Bruno's
formula is the all-orders chain rule.


Smoothness is more than this formula needs. The \(n\)-th order statement
requires \(n\) derivatives of \(g\) near \(x\) and \(n\) derivatives of \(f\)
near \(g(x)\). At \(n=1\), the formula is exactly the chain rule.


The tuple \((k_1,\ldots,k_n)\) records an integer partition of \(n\): \(k_m\)
is the number of parts of size \(m\). The coefficient
\[
  \frac{n!}{\prod_m k_m!\,(m!)^{k_m}}
\]
counts set partitions with that block-size profile. The outer derivative
\(f^{(k)}\) is differentiated once per block, while each block of size \(m\)
contributes one factor \(g^{(m)}\).


The formula uses the bare-product normalization: the coefficient contains
\((m!)^{k_m}\), and the product contains \(\bigl(g^{(m)}(x)\bigr)^{k_m}\).
Equivalently, one may put \(g^{(m)}(x)/m!\) inside the product and remove
\((m!)^{k_m}\) from the denominator. Mixing these two conventions gives the
wrong coefficients.


The constraint \(\sum_m mk_m=n\) is precisely the multiplicity form of an
integer partition of \(n\). Thus the number of summands is \(p(n)\), the
partition function from the discrete and number-system material, now
appearing as bookkeeping for iterated differentiation.


This theorem is enrichment, not a critical dependency for the integration,
measure, or manifold arcs. It is included because it is the complete
all-orders chain rule and a useful callback to partitions.
